The fifth: If you mock us, then we seek Allah's help against you. He called this mockery so that the two expressions would correspond, as we explained regarding His saying ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:15]. This is the saying of Ibn al-Anbari.

Ibn Abbas said: Before the Flood there was neither river nor sea on earth, which is why they mocked him. The waters of the seas are only a remnant of the Flood.

(p-104) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So you will soon know﴾. This is a warning, and its meaning is: "So you will soon know who is more deserving of mockery, and who has the better end."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Upon whom will come a punishment that will disgrace him﴾, that is, will humiliate him, and it is drowning. ﴿And there will descend upon him﴾, that is, there will be obligated upon him, ﴿a lasting punishment﴾ in the Hereafter.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verse 40:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Until when Our command came﴾. Concerning it there are two opinions. The first: "Our command came" means Our command to punish them and destroy them. The second: "Our punishment came," which was the water. It began at the edges of the earth and encircled it like a crown, and rain began to fall from the sky like the mouths of waterskins. The wild animals began seeking the middle of the earth, fleeing from the water, until they gathered around the ship. At that point he carried in it two of every kind.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the oven gushed forth﴾. Al-fawr (gushing) is boiling; al-fawwara is what bubbles up from the pot, as said by Ibn Faris.

The author (al-Musannif) said: I read to our shaykh Abu Mansur al-Lughawi, from Ibn Durayd, who said: "al-tannur" is a Persian word that has been Arabized; the Arabs know no name for it other than this, and therefore it came in the revelation, since they were addressed with what they knew. It is related from Ibn Abbas that he said: "al-tannur" is in every Arabic and non-Arabic tongue.

Concerning the meaning of this tannur there are six opinions:

The first: that it is a name for the surface of the earth. Ikrimah related it from Ali, peace be upon him. al-Dahhak related from Ibn Abbas: "al-tannur" is the surface of the earth. He said: it was said to him: when you see the water has risen over the surface of the earth, board the ship, you and your companions. This is also the saying of Ikrimah and al-Zuhri.

The second: that it is the brightening of the dawn (tanwir al-subh). Abu Juhayfa related it from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him. Ibn Qutaybah said: "al-tanwir" is at the time of prayer.

The third: that it is the rising of dawn (tulu al-fajr). It is related from Ali also, who said: "And the oven gushed forth" means the dawn rose.

The fourth: that it is the rising of the sun (tulu al-shams), also transmitted from Ali.

The fifth: that it is the oven of his family. al-Awfi related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "When you see the oven of your family gushing forth water, then it is the destruction of your people." Abu Salih related from Ibn Abbas that it was the oven of Adam, peace be upon him, which Allah gave to Nuh, and it was said to him: when water gushes from it, carry what you have been commanded. al-Hasan said: it was an oven of stone. This is the saying of Mujahid, al-Farra', and Muqatil.

The sixth: that it is the highest and most elevated part of the earth.

Ibn al-Anbari said: the high parts of the earth and its elevated places were likened to ovens because of their height. They differed concerning the place from which the oven gushed forth, on three opinions:

The first: that it gushed forth from the mosque of Kufa. Habba al-Urani related it from Ali, peace be upon him. Zirr ibn Hubaysh said: the oven gushed forth from the right corner of the mosque of Kufa. Mujahid said: the water sprang from the oven, and his wife knew of it and informed him, and that was in the region of Kufa. al-Sha'bi used to swear by Allah that the tannur was only in the region of Kufa.

The second: that it gushed forth in India. Ikrimah related it from Ibn Abbas.

The third: that it was at the farthest end of Nuh's house, which was in Syria, in a place called 'Ayn Warda. Muqatil said so.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We said: Carry in it﴾, that is, in the ship, ﴿of every kind two, a pair﴾. Hafs related from Asim: "min kullin" with tanwin. Abu Ali said: the meaning is "of every thing," and "of every pair two," so the governed noun was omitted. "Ithnayn" is in the accusative as an attribute of "zawjayn," and it is known that the two pairs are two, but it is for emphasis. Mujahid said: of every species, male and female. Ibn Qutaybah said: the zawj may be one, and may be two; here it is one, and the meaning of the verse is: carry of every male and female two. al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: carry two pairs of every thing; in Arabic usage, zawj may have a single companion, and two may be called zawjan; one says, "I have two zawjan of birds," meaning only a male and a female. Ibn al-Anbari said: he said "ithnayn" and made the zawj dual because he intended the male and female of the animals, and its implied sense is: of every male and female.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your family﴾, that is, carry your family. The exegetes said that by his family he meant his dependents and his offspring. ﴿Except those against whom the word has already gone forth﴾, that is, against whom the word from Allah had already gone forth regarding destruction. al-Dahhak said: they were his wife and his son Kan'an.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who believed﴾, its meaning: carry those who believed. ﴿And none believed with him except a few.﴾ Concerning their number there are eight opinions:

The first: that they were eighty men with their families. Ikrimah related it from Ibn Abbas.

The second: that Nuh carried with him eighty persons, his three sons, three wives for his sons, and Nuh's wife. Yusuf ibn Mihran related it from Ibn Abbas.

The third: they were eighty persons, said by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. Muqatil said they were forty men and forty women.

The fourth: they were forty, mentioned by Ibn Jurayj from Ibn Abbas.

The fifth: they were thirty men, related by Abu Nuhayk from Ibn Abbas.

The sixth: they were eight. al-Hakam ibn Utayba said: Nuh and his three sons and four daughters-in-law. Qatada said: it was mentioned to us that none was saved in the ship except Nuh, his wife, three sons, and their wives; their total is eight. This is the saying of al-Qurazi and Ibn Jurayj.

The seventh: they were seven: Nuh, three of his wives, and three sons. This was said by al-A'mash.

The eighth: they were ten besides their women, said by Ibn Ishaq. It is related from him that he said: those who were saved with Nuh were his three sons, their three wives, and six from among those who believed in him.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 11, verse 41:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And he said﴾, meaning Noah, to those he was commanded to carry: ﴿Board it﴾, the ship. Ibn 'Abbas said: They boarded it on the tenth of Rajab, and they disembarked from it on the Day of 'Ashura'. Ibn Jurayj said: It (the ship) was lifted from the spring of Warda on Friday, on the tenth of Rajab, and it came to the site of the House (the Ka'bah), and it circled around it seven times, and the House had been raised at that time. It came to rest at Baqirdi, upon al-Judi, on the Day of 'Ashura'. Ibn 'Abbas also said: A mouse gnawed at the ropes of the ship, so Noah complained of that. God Exalted revealed to him, and he rubbed the tail of the lion, and two cats emerged. There was dung in the ship, so he complained of that to his Lord, and God Exalted revealed to him, and he rubbed the tail of the elephant, and two pigs emerged and ate that.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿In the name of God is its course and its mooring﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "mujraha" (مُجْراها) with a ḍammah on the mim. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read "majrahā" (مَجْرِاها) with a fatḥah on the mim and a kasrah on the ra'. All of them read "murssaha" (مُرْساها) with a ḍammah on the mim, except that Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs from 'Asim used a fatḥah on the sin. Nafi' and Abu Bakr from 'Asim recited it between the kasrah and the tafkhim (a heavy, rounded pronunciation). Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf used imalah (a vowel inclination toward the i-sound). None of these readers made it an attribute (na't) of God. Rather, al-Hasan, Qatadah, Humayd al-A'raj, and Isma'il ibn Mujalid from 'Asim made both descriptive words an attribute of God Exalted, and they read "mujriha wa-mursiha" (مُجْرِيها ومُرْسِيها) with a ḍammah on the mim and two sound yā's, like "mubdiha wa-munshiha" (مُبْدِيها ومُنْشِيها). Ibn Mas'ud read "majraha" with a fatḥah on the mim and imalah of the ra' followed by an alif, and "mursaha" with a ḍammah on the mim and imalah of the sin followed by an alif. Abu Razin and Abu al-Mutawakkil read "majraha" with a fatḥah on the mim and the ra', with an alif after it, and "mursaha" with a ḍammah on the mim and a fatḥah on the sin, with an alif after it. Abu al-Jawza' and Ibn Ya'mar read "majraha wa-marsaha" with a fatḥah on the mim in both, and a fatḥah on the ra' and the sin, with an alif after both. (p-109) Yahya ibn Wathhab read with a fatḥah on both mims, except that he used imalah on the ra' and the sin in both words. Abu 'Imran al-Jawni and Ibn Jubayr read with a ḍammah on the mim in both, a fatḥah on the ra' and the sin, and an alif after both.

Whoever reads with a ḍammah on both mims derives it from ajra and arsa (the causative forms). Whoever reads with a fatḥah on both takes it as a verbal noun (maṣdar) from jara al-shay'u yajri majran (the thing ran, flowed) and rasa yarsi marsan (it anchored). Al-Zajjaj said: His saying "In the name of God" means "by God," and the meaning is that He commanded them to invoke His name at the time of its running and at the time of its stopping.

As for whoever reads with a ḍammah on both mims, the meaning is: by God is its running, and by God is its anchoring. Whoever reads with a fatḥah on both, the meaning is: by God its running occurs, and by God its anchoring, that is, its settling, takes place. I heard our shaykh Abu Mansur al-Lughawi say: Whoever reads the mim in "majraha" with a ḍammah intends: God caused it to run a course (ajraha Allahu mujran). Whoever reads it with a fatḥah intends: it ran a course (jarat majran). Al-Dahhak said: Whenever he wanted it to run, he would say: "In the name of God," and it would run. And whenever he wanted it to anchor, he would say: "In the name of God," and it would anchor.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verses 42–43:

Allah's words: ﴿And it sailed with them through waves like mountains﴾. He likened them to mountains in their immensity and height. It is said that the water rose above the tallest mountain on earth by forty cubits, and it is narrated as fifteen cubits. Some exegetes mentioned that it rose toward the sky seventy farsakh (parasangs) above the earth.

Allah's words: ﴿And Noah called out to his son﴾. There is no disagreement that he was a disbeliever. Regarding his name there are two opinions:

The first: Kan'an (Kan'an), which is the view of the majority. The second: his name was Yam, as related by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and this was also the view of 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr and Ibn Ishaq.

Allah's words: ﴿And he was apart﴾. Al-ma'zil (the isolated place) is the place that is cut off, and the meaning of al-'azl is removal. There are two interpretations of the meaning, mentioned by al-Zajjaj:

The first: in a place apart from the ship. The second: in a place apart from the religion of his father.

Allah's words: ﴿O my son, board with us﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "Ya bunayya irkab" with the word in the idafa form, with the ya vowelled with kasra. Abu Bakr narrated from 'Asim "Ya bunayya" with the ya fathah here, while the rest of the Qur'an has kasra. Hafs narrated from him fathah throughout the Qur'an for "Ya bunayya" when it is singular. The grammarians said: the original form of "bunayya" (diminutive of "ibn", little son) has three ya's: the ya of diminutive (ya al-tasghir), a ya after it which is the radical of the verb (lam al-fi'l), and a ya after the radical which is the ya of possession (ya al-idafa). Whoever reads "Ya bunayyi" intends "Ya bunayyi-ya," deleting the ya of possession and leaving the kasra to indicate it, as one says "Ya ghulamu aqbil" (O boy, come). Whoever vowels the ya with fathah replaces the kasra of the radical with a fathah, to avoid the heaviness of gathering ya's with a kasra; the ya of possession then turns into an alif, and then the alif is deleted as a ya would be deleted, leaving the fathah in its state. It is also said that the meaning is: "Ya bunayya, have faith and board with us."

Allah's words: ﴿I will take refuge﴾, that is: I will go and retreat ﴿to a mountain that will protect me﴾, that is: will prevent me ﴿from the water﴾, that is: from the water's drowning.

Allah's words: ﴿He said, "There is no protector today"﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

The first: there is no preventer today from the command of Allah, as said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: there is no one protected. A similar usage is "water gushing" (ma' dafiq), meaning poured out, and "a hidden secret" (sirr katim), and "a sleeping night" (layl na'im), as said by Ibn Qutaybah.

Allah's words: ﴿except for him on whom Allah has mercy﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: this is an exception not from the first (group), and the meaning is: but whomever Allah has mercy on, he is protected. Muqatil said: except whomever He has mercy on, so he boarded the ship.

Allah's words: ﴿And the wave came between them﴾. Regarding the referent of the pronoun there are two opinions:

The first: they are the son and the mountain that he claimed would protect him, related by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and this was also the view of Mujahid. The second: they are Noah and his son, said by Muqatil.

Allah's words: ﴿And it sailed with them through waves like mountains﴾. He likened them to mountains in their immensity and height. It is said that the water rose above the tallest mountain on earth by forty cubits, and it is narrated as fifteen cubits. Allah's words: ﴿He said, "There is no protector today"﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

The first: there is no preventer today from the command of Allah, as said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: there is no one protected. A similar usage is "water gushing" (ma' dafiq), meaning poured out, and "a hidden secret" (sirr katim), and "a sleeping night" (layl na'im), as said by Ibn Qutaybah.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verses 44–47:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And it was said, "O earth, swallow your water"﴾. A group stopped at the apparent meaning of the verse and said: "It only swallowed what gushed out of it, and did not swallow the water of the sky. That water became seas and rivers." This is the meaning of the saying of Ibn 'Abbas. Others held that what is meant is: "Swallow the water that is upon you," which is what gushed from the earth and what descended from the sky, and this was after everything on the surface of the earth had drowned.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And, "O sky, withhold"﴾, meaning: hold back from sending down water. Ibn al-Anbari said: Since the mention of water had already preceded, it is understood that the meaning is: "Withhold from sending down water."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the water subsided﴾, meaning: it decreased. Al-Zajjaj said: It is said *ghada al-ma'u yaghīdu* (the water subsided, *yaghīdu*) when it sank into the earth. It is permissible to use *ishmam* (*ishmām*, the rounding of the lips with a *ḍamma* while pronouncing the consonant, here the *ghayn*, in a way that indicates the *ḍamma*) with the *ḍamma* on the *ghayn*.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the matter was decided﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: Whoever was to drown drowned, and whoever was to be saved was saved. Mujahid said: "The matter was decided" means the destruction of the people of Noah. Ibn Qutayba said: "And the matter was decided" (p-112) means: it was finished. Ibn al-Anbari said: The meaning is that the destruction of the people of Noah was made final. Since the narrative had already shown what their destruction was, there was no need to describe the matter further.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And it came to rest﴾, meaning the ship, ﴿upon al-Judi﴾, which is the name of a mountain. Al-A'mash and Ibn Abi 'Abla read *"ʿalā al-Jūdī"* with the *yā'* sukun (without the shadda). Ibn al-Anbari said: The *yā'* in *al-Jūdiyy* is doubled because it is the *yā' al-nisba* (the *nisba* yā', the suffix of relation), so it is like the *yā'* in *ʿalawiyy* and *hāshimiyy*. Some reciters have lightened it, and among the Arabs there are those who lighten the *nisba* yā' by making it sukun in the nominative and genitive, and by making it a fatha in the accusative, so they say: *qāma Zaydun al-ʿalawī* and *ra'aytu Zaydan al-ʿalawiya*.

Ibn 'Abbas said: The ship circled around the House forty days, then God directed it toward al-Judi, and it came to rest upon it.

They differed as to where this mountain is, in three opinions:

The first: that it is in Mosul. This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Dahhak said the same.

The second: that it is in al-Jazira. This was said by Mujahid and Qatada. Muqatil said: It is in al-Jazira, near Mosul.

The third: that it is in the region of Amid. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

Regarding the reason it came to rest upon it, there are two opinions:

One: that it did not drown, because the mountains had risen high and grown tall that day, while it humbled itself and so did not drown, and so it settled upon it. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: that when the water decreased, it settled upon it, so its resting upon it was a sign of the scarcity of the water.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And it was said, "Away with the wrongdoing people!"﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: Away from the mercy of God for the disbelieving people.

(p-113) If it is asked: What is the sin of those among the animals and children who were drowned?

The answer: Their appointed terms had arrived, so they were made to die by drowning. This was said by al-Dahhak and Ibn Juraij.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿My Lord, indeed my son is of my family﴾. Noah only said this because God had promised him the salvation of his family, and so He said: ﴿And indeed Your promise is the truth, and You are the most just of judges.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: the most just of the just. Ibn Zayd said: You are the judge most fair with truth.

They differed concerning this matter about which Noah asked, in two opinions:

One: that he was the son of Noah by his loins. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and the majority.

The second: that he was born on his bed but was not his son, being of illegitimate birth. Ibn al-Anbari related with his chain from al-Hasan that he said: He was not his son; his wife committed adultery. And from al-Sha'bi he said: He was not his son; his wife betrayed him. And from Mujahid something similar. Ibn Juraij said: Noah called to him while he thought he was his son, for he had been born on his bed. According to the first opinion, the meaning of His saying: ﴿Indeed, he is not of your family﴾ has two interpretations:

One: he is not of your religion.

The second: he is not of your family whose salvation I promised you. Ibn 'Abbas said: The wife of a prophet never committed adultery; rather the meaning is: he is not of your family whose salvation I promised you. As for the second opinion (p-114), the speech is according to its apparent meaning. The first opinion is more correct, because it agrees with the apparent meaning of the Qur'an and because the majority agree upon it, and it is preferable to accusing a prophet's wife of immorality.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, it is an act other than righteous﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Hamza read: ﴿Indeed, it is ʿamalun﴾ with tanwin and raf' (nominative), ﴿ghayru ṣāliḥin﴾ with the *ra'* in the nominative. There are two opinions regarding this:

One: that it refers back to the request concerning it. The meaning is: your asking me about it is an act other than righteous. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada, and this is apparent, because the request concerning him had already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿My Lord, indeed my son is of my family﴾, so the pronoun returns to it.

The second: that it refers back to the thing asked about.

Regarding this meaning there are two opinions: One: that he was of illegitimate birth. This was said by al-Hasan. The second: that the meaning is: he is one of an act other than righteous. This was said by al-Zajjaj. Ibn al-Anbari said: Whoever says he was of illegitimate birth says the meaning is: the origin of your son, whom you think is your son, is an act other than righteous. Whoever says he is "one of an act other than righteous" says: the noun that is being modified has been omitted and the act has been put in its place, as the Arabs say: *ʿAbdu Allāh iqbālun wa idbārun*, meaning: "the possessor of advance and retreat." Al-Kisa'i read *"ʿamila"* with a kasra on the *mīm* and fatha on the *lām*, *"ghayra ṣāliḥin"* with fatha on the *ra'*, indicating that he is a polytheist.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So do not ask Me about that of which you have no knowledge﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and Ibn 'Amir read: *"fa-lā tasalanna"* with fatha on the *lām* and shadda on the *nūn*; except that Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir put a kasra on the *nūn*, and Ibn Kathir put a fatha on it, and they omitted the *yā'* in both connected and pausal speech. ʿAsim, Abu 'Amr, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read with sukun on the *lām* and lightening of the *nūn*, except that Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far (p-115) affirmed the *yā'* in connected speech and omitted it in pausal speech, and Ya'qub paused on it with the *yā'*, while the rest omit it in both states. Abu 'Ali said: Whoever puts a kasra on the *nūn* has transitively extended the verb "ask" to two objects: one is the first-person pronoun, and the other is the relative noun. The *nūn* attached to the first-person *yā'* was dropped because of the gathering of *nūns*. As for affirming the *yā'* in connected speech, that is the original form, and omitting it is lighter, and the kasra indicates it, and makes known that the object is intended in meaning.

Then, regarding the meaning of the speech, there are three opinions:

One: that it is his attribution of him to himself while he is not of him.

The second: in his inclusion of him within the body of his family whose salvation He had promised him.

The third: his request for the rescue of an unbeliever from the punishment.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, I admonish you, lest you be among the ignorant﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions:

One: that you be among the ignorant in asking about one who is not of your party.

Then He mentioned the disbelievers, saying: ﴿And nations﴾, i.e., from the descendants also, and the meaning is: and among those whom We describe to you there are nations, and among those whose account We relate to you there are nations. ﴿We will grant them enjoyment﴾, i.e., in this world, ﴿then a painful punishment will touch them from Us﴾ in the Hereafter. Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi said: On that day, no believing man or believing woman remained in the loins of men and the wombs of women until the Hour is established except that they entered into that peace and those blessings; and no disbeliever remained except that he entered into that enjoyment and punishment."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verse 49–53:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That is from the news of the unseen﴾ — regarding what is referred to by "that" (tilka), there are two opinions:

One of them: it is the story of Noah. The second: it is the verses of the Qur'an. The meaning is: that is from the reports of what was hidden from you and from your people.

If it is said: why does He say here "tilka" (that, feminine), while in another place He says "dhalika" (that, masculine)?

Ibn al-Anbari has answered this, saying: "tilka" refers to the verses of the Qur'an, and "dhalika" refers to the report and the account. Both are well known in the eloquent language. A man says, "So-and-so has arrived," and the listener to his words says, "I am pleased with it" (qad faraḥtu bihi) and "I am delighted by it" (qad surirtu bihā). When he uses the masculine, he means the arrival; when he uses the feminine, he has in mind the "arrival" (qadmah) as a thing.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿before this﴾ — meaning the Qur'an. ﴿So be patient﴾ as Noah was patient over the harm of his people. ﴿Indeed, the final outcome﴾ — that is, the ultimate result, with victory and establishment ﴿is for the God-conscious﴾ — that is, for you and your people, just as it was for the believers among the people of Noah.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿You are nothing but fabricators﴾ — that is, you are nothing but liars in your associating the idols with Allah. As for what follows this, its explanation has already preceded [Yunus: 72], up to His saying: ﴿He will send the sky upon you in abundant rain﴾, and this too has already had its explanation given in Surah [al-An'am: 61]. The reason for His saying this to them is that Allah withheld the rain from them for three years and made the wombs of their women barren, so He promised them the revival of their lands and the expansion of provision for them if they believed.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And He will add strength to your strength﴾ — regarding this there are three opinions:

One of them: it is children and grandchildren; this was related by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas.

The second: He will increase you in might to your might; this was said by Mujahid and Ibn Zayd.

The third: abundance upon your abundance; this was said by al-Dahhak.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do not turn away as criminals﴾ — Muqatil said: do not turn away from monotheism as polytheists.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿You have not brought us any clear proof﴾ — that is, any evident argument. ﴿And we will not abandon our gods﴾ — meaning the idols. ﴿on your word﴾ — that is, "bi-qawlika" (on account of your word); the "bā'" (ba) and "ʿan" interchange in meaning.

(p-118) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We say not but that some of our gods have struck you with madness﴾. That is, what we say concerning the cause of your opposition to us is only that some of our gods have afflicted you with madness because of your reviling them; so what you display of their defects is due to the change that has befallen your intellect. Ibn Qutayba said: one says ʿarānī kadhā and iʿtarānī (it befell me, it overtook me) when it visits a person. From this comes the saying of one who comes to you seeking your gift: ʿāriyy (a visitor/seeker). And from it is the verse of al-Nabigha:

"I came to you as a visitor, my garments worn thin, in fear, while suspicions are imputed to me."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed I call Allah to witness﴾ to the end of the verse. Nāfiʿ vocalized the yāʾ of "innī" (with a movement). The meaning of the verse: if you say, "Our gods have punished me for my disparaging them," then I am certain of their defectiveness and of my disavowal of them, and here I am increasing my disparagement of them. ﴿So scheme against me, all of you together﴾, that is: plot, you and your idols, against my harm, then do not give me respite. Al-Zajjaj said: This is among the greatest signs of the messengers, that the messenger is alone while his community is united against him, yet he says to them, "Scheme against me," and none of them is able to harm him. Likewise Noah said to his people: ﴿So resolve upon your affair, and your associates﴾ [Yunus: 71]. And Muhammad (ﷺ) said: ﴿If you have a scheme, then scheme against me﴾ [al-Mursalat: 39].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿There is no creature but that He holds its forelock﴾. Abu ʿUbayda said: the meaning is that it is in His grasp, His dominion, and His authority.

If it is asked: Why did He specify the forelock?

The answer: the forelock (nāṣiyah) is the hair of the front of the head. When you take hold of a person by it, you have gained control over the rest of his body, and he is subdued to you.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed my Lord is upon a straight path﴾. Mujahid said: upon the truth. Others said: there is an implied element in the speech, its estimate being: indeed my Lord guides to a straight path.

(p-119) If it is asked: What is the connection between His saying, "There is no creature but that He holds its forelock," and His being upon a straight path? There are two answers to this:

The first: when He informed that He holds the forelocks of creation, its meaning was that they do not escape His grasp; so He informed that He is upon a way from which no fleeing one deviates, and from which no hidden one is concealed from Him.

The second: the meaning is that although He is capable over them, He does not wrong them, and wills only justice. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned both.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verse 57:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But if you turn away﴾, there are two views:

The first: it is a past-tense verb, meaning: "If they turn away." According to this, there is an omission (idmar) in the verse, its summary being: "If they turn away, then say to them: I have already conveyed to you." This is the view of Muqatil and others.

The second: it is an address to those present, and its underlying form is "fa-in tatawallaw" (if you turn away). They found it burdensome to combine two moving taa' (tā'), so one of them was kept and the other dropped, as al-Nabigha said:

"The man desires to live long, and long life may harm him;
its brightness fades, and bitter remains after sweet living.
And the days turn about until he sees nothing that pleases him."

He intended: "wa-tatasarrafu al-ayyam" (and the days turn about), so he dropped one of the two taa's. This was related by Ibn al-Anbari.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And my Lord will replace you with another people﴾, there is in it a threat to them of destruction. ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Guardian over all things﴾, there are two views on it:

The first: "Guardian" over the deeds of the servants until He recompenses them for them. The second: that "ʿalā" (upon) carries the meaning of "lām" (for), so the meaning is: "for every thing there is a guardian," and so He protects me from your reaching me with harm.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verse 58:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when Our command came﴾ — there are two views concerning it:

One of them: "Our punishment came." This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: "Our command came" means Our command for their destruction.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We saved Hud and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us﴾ — there are two views concerning it:

One of them: "We saved them from the punishment by Our favor." The second: "We saved them by guiding them to faith and protecting them from disbelief." Both views are reported from Ibn ʿAbbas.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We saved them from a severe punishment﴾ — i.e., harsh (shadid). This is what the people of Hud deserved of the punishment of this world and the Hereafter.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verse 59:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And that was ʿĀd﴾, meaning the tribe. ﴿And they disobeyed His messengers﴾. One might say: Hūd was sent to them alone, so how is it mentioned with the plural form?

(p-121) The answer comes in three aspects:

The first: the plural form may be mentioned while a single person is meant, as in His saying: ﴿Or do they envy the people?﴾ [al-Nisa, 54], where what is meant is the Prophet (ﷺ) alone.

The second: whoever denies one messenger has denied all of them.

The third: each time he warned them was a renewed message, and he was a messenger in it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And followed﴾, meaning the followers followed the command of the leaders.

Al-Jabbar (the tyrant) is one who is high and out of reach of the hand.

The scholars have four opinions concerning al-Jabbar:

The first: he is the one who kills in anger and punishes in anger; this was said by al-Kalbi.

The second: he is the one who compels people to what he wills; this was said by al-Zajjaj.

The third: he is the one who holds authority over others.

The fourth: he is the one who is great in himself and arrogant towards the servants; Ibn al-Anbari mentioned these two. What we have mentioned encompasses these opinions, and we have expanded on this explanation at [al-Ma'idah, 22].

As for al-ʿAnid (the obstinate): he is the one who does not accept the truth. Ibn Qutaybah said: al-ʿAnud, al-ʿAnid and al-ʿAnid (the stubborn opponent) are those who oppose you with dissent against you.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verses 60–69:**

God's words: ﴿And they were followed in this world by a curse﴾, meaning: a curse was attached to them, accompanying them. ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection﴾, meaning: on the Day of Resurrection they will also be cursed. ﴿Indeed, ʿAd disbelieved in their Lord﴾, meaning: disbelieved *in* their Lord, so the preposition *bāʾ* was dropped. They recited:

*Verse:* "I commanded you to do good, so do what you were commanded, / for I have left you possessing wealth and property."

Al-Zajjaj said: His words ﴿Alā (Indeed/Surely)﴾ are an opening and an alert, and ﴿Buʿdan (far away)﴾ is in the accusative on the sense of: "May God distance them," so they were distanced, a distancing, meaning: He removed them from His mercy.

God's words: ﴿He brought you into being from the earth﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

One: He created you from Adam, and Adam was created from the earth. The second: He brought you into being in the earth.

Regarding His words ﴿and made you inhabit it﴾ there are three opinions:

The second opinion: "So you increase me in nothing but ruin if I return to your religion." This is the meaning of Muqatil's statement.

When they awoke on the second day, their faces were red, so they wailed and wept. When they awoke on the third day, their faces were black, as if they had been smeared with pitch, so they all cried out: "Surely the punishment has come upon you!" They prepared their shrouds and threw themselves on the ground, not knowing from where the punishment would come to them. When they awoke on the fourth day, a cry came to them from the sky containing the sound of every thunderbolt, and their hearts were torn apart within their chests. Muqatil said: they dug graves for themselves. When the sun rose on the fourth day and the punishment had not come to them, they thought God had had mercy on them, so they came out of their graves calling to one another, when Gabriel descended and stood above the city, blocking the light of the sun. When they saw him, they went back into their graves. He cried out to them with a shout: "Die where you are; the curse of God be upon you!" Their souls departed, their houses shook, and they fell upon their graves.

Al-Zajjaj said: His words ﴿Alā (Indeed/Surely)﴾ are an opening and an alert, and ﴿Buʿdan (far away)﴾ is in the accusative on the sense of: "May God distance them," so they were distanced, a distancing, meaning: He removed them from His mercy.

God's words: ﴿He brought you into being from the earth﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

One: He created you from Adam, and Adam was created from the earth. The second: He brought you into being in the earth.

One: He made you settle in it (*aʿmarakum fīhā*), that is, made you its inhabitants for the duration of your lives, and from this comes *ʿumrā* (the grant of a dwelling for life). This is the opinion of Mujahid.

The second: He prolonged your lives. Their lifespans were from a thousand years down to three hundred. This was said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

The third: He made you its cultivators (*ʿammārahā*). This was said by Abu ʿUbayda.

God's words: ﴿You were indeed a man in whom we had hope before this﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions:

One: They used to hope he would become their king after their kingship, because he had noble lineage and wealth. This was said by Kaʿb.

The second: He used to hate their idols and turn away from their religion, and they hoped he would return to their religion. When he declared their warning, their hope in him was cut off. Muqatil took a similar view.

The third: They used to hope for his good. When he warned them, they claimed their hope in his good had been cut off. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

God's words: ﴿And indeed we are in doubt﴾. If someone asks: why did He say here *wa-innanā* ("and indeed we") while in (Ibrahim) He said *wa-innā* ("and indeed we")?

Al-Farraʾ said: whoever says *innanā* keeps the particle in its original form, because the first-person plural suffix is *nā*, so three *nūn*s come together: the *nūn* of *inna* and the *nūn* attached to the *alif*. Whoever says *innā* finds the joining of three *nūn*s heavy, so he drops the third and keeps the first two. Similarly one says *innī* and *innanī*, *laʿallī* and *laʿallanī*, *laytī* and *laytanī*. *Verse:* "Show me a steed that died of emaciation, perhaps I [may] / see what you see, or a miserly, eternally [wealthy] one."

*Verse:* "Like the wish of Jabir when he said, 'Oh, if only I might encounter him / and spend some of my wealth.'"

*Verse:* "I commanded you to do good, so do what you were commanded, / for I have left you possessing wealth and property."

Al-Zajjaj said: His words ﴿Alā (Indeed/Surely)﴾ are an opening and an alert, and ﴿Buʿdan (far away)﴾ is in the accusative on the sense of: "May God distance them," so they were distanced, a distancing, meaning: He removed them from His mercy.

God's words: ﴿He brought you into being from the earth﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

One: He created you from Adam, and Adam was created from the earth. The second: He brought you into being in the earth.

Regarding His words ﴿and made you inhabit it﴾ there are three opinions:

One: He made you settle in it (*aʿmarakum fīhā*), that is, made you its inhabitants for the duration of your lives, and from this comes *ʿumrā* (the grant of a dwelling for life). This is the opinion of Mujahid.

The second: He prolonged your lives. Their lifespans were from a thousand years down to three hundred. This was said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

The third: He made you its cultivators (*ʿammārahā*). This was said by Abu ʿUbayda.

God's words: ﴿You were indeed a man in whom we had hope before this﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions:

One: They used to hope he would become their king after their kingship, because he had noble lineage and wealth. This was said by Kaʿb.

The second: He used to hate their idols and turn away from their religion, and they hoped he would return to their religion. When he declared their warning, their hope in him was cut off. Muqatil took a similar view.

The third: They used to hope for his good. When he warned them, they claimed their hope in his good had been cut off. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

God's words: ﴿And indeed we are in doubt﴾. If someone asks: why did He say here *wa-innanā* ("and indeed we") while in (Ibrahim) He said *wa-innā* ("and indeed we")?

The answer: both are dialects among the seven dialects of Quraysh in which the Qur'an was revealed. Al-Farraʾ said: whoever says *innanā* keeps the particle in its original form, because the first-person plural suffix is *nā*, so three *nūn*s come together: the *nūn* of *inna* and the *nūn* attached to the *alif*. Whoever says *innā* finds the joining of three *nūn*s heavy, so he drops the third and keeps the first two. Similarly one says *innī* and *innanī*, *laʿallī* and *laʿallanī*, *laytī* and *laytanī*. God said in the higher dialect: ﴿Perhaps I may reach the means﴾ [Ghafir: 36], and a poet said in the other dialect:

*Verse:* "Show me a steed that died of emaciation, perhaps I [may] / see what you see, or a miserly, eternally [wealthy] one."

And God said: ﴿Oh, I wish I had been with them﴾ [al-Nisa: 73], and a poet said:

*Verse:* "Like the wish of Jabir when he said, 'Oh, if only I might encounter him / and spend some of my wealth.'"

As for *al-murīb* (the one who causes doubt), it means the one who causes suspicion and accusation. And "mercy" here is intended to mean prophethood.

God's words: ﴿So you increase me in nothing but loss﴾. *Takhsīr* means decrease.

Regarding the meaning of the statement there are two opinions:

One: "So you increase me in nothing but a clear perception of your own loss." This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. Al-Farraʾ said: the meaning is "so you increase me in nothing but loss *for you*," that is, whenever you offer me an excuse, it only increases your loss. Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: "nothing but loss *for you*, not for me." Some said: the meaning is "you increase me by what you have said only in attributing you to loss."

The second opinion: "So you increase me in nothing but ruin if I return to your religion." This is the meaning of Muqatil's statement.

If it is said: the apparent meaning of this is that he was in loss, and they increased his loss. We have already given the answer regarding His words: ﴿Had they gone out among you, they would have increased you in nothing but corruption﴾ [al-Tawba: 47].

God's words: ﴿This is the she-camel of God for you as a sign﴾. We have explained it in the surah of al-Aʿraf [73].

God's words: ﴿Enjoy yourselves in your homes﴾, that is: enjoy your lives. He expressed life by *tamattuʿ* (enjoyment), because the living are enjoying through the senses.

God's words: ﴿for three days﴾. The exegetes said: when the she-camel was hamstrung, her young went up the mountain and cried out three times. Salih said: "For every cry there is a term of one day. When they awoke on the second day, their faces were red, so they wailed and wept. When they awoke on the third day, their faces were black, as if they had been smeared with pitch, so they all cried out: "Surely the punishment has come upon you!" They prepared their shrouds and threw themselves on the ground, not knowing from where the punishment would come to them. When they awoke on the fourth day, a cry came to them from the sky containing the sound of every thunderbolt, and their hearts were torn apart within their chests. Muqatil said: they dug graves for themselves. When the sun rose on the fourth day and the punishment had not come to them, they thought God had had mercy on them, so they came out of their graves calling to one another, when Gabriel descended and stood above the city, blocking the light of the sun. When they saw him, they went back into their graves. He cried out to them with a shout: "Die where you are; the curse of God be upon you!" Their souls departed, their houses shook, and they fell upon their graves.

God's words: ﴿And from the disgrace of that day﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr and Ibn ʿAmir recited *yawmiʾidhin* with a kasra on the *mīm*. al-Kisaʾi recited it with a fatha on the *mīm* with the annexation (*iḍāfa*). He said: He only said *wa-akhadha* ("and seized") because the cry is taken to mean the shouting.

Al-Zajjaj said: His words ﴿Alā (Indeed/Surely)﴾ are an opening and an alert, and ﴿Buʿdan (far away)﴾ is in the accusative on the sense of: "May God distance them," so they were distanced, a distancing, meaning: He removed them from His mercy.

God's words: ﴿He brought you into being from the earth﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

One: He created you from Adam, and Adam was created from the earth. The second: He brought you into being in the earth.

Regarding His words ﴿and made you inhabit it﴾ there are three opinions:

One: He made you settle in it (*aʿmarakum fīhā*), that is, made you its inhabitants for the duration of your lives, and from this comes *ʿumrā* (the grant of a dwelling for life). This is the opinion of Mujahid.

The second: He prolonged your lives. Their lifespans were from a thousand years down to three hundred. This was said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

The third: He made you its cultivators (*ʿammārahā*). This was said by Abu ʿUbayda.

God's words: ﴿You were indeed a man in whom we had hope before this﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions:

One: They used to hope he would become their king after their kingship, because he had noble lineage and wealth. This was said by Kaʿb.

The second: He used to hate their idols and turn away from their religion, and they hoped he would return to their religion. When he declared their warning, their hope in him was cut off. Muqatil took a similar view.

The third: They used to hope for his good. When he warned them, they claimed their hope in his good had been cut off. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

God's words: ﴿And indeed we are in doubt﴾. If someone asks: why did He say here *wa-innanā* ("and indeed we") while in (Ibrahim) He said *wa-innā* ("and indeed we")?

The answer: both are dialects among the seven dialects of Quraysh in which the Qur'an was revealed. Al-Farraʾ said: whoever says *innanā* keeps the particle in its original form, because the first-person plural suffix is *nā*, so three *nūn*s come together: the *nūn* of *inna* and the *nūn* attached to the *alif*. Whoever says *innā* finds the joining of three *nūn*s heavy, so he drops the third and keeps the first two. Similarly one says *innī* and *innanī*, *laʿallī* and *laʿallanī*, *laytī* and *laytanī*. God said in the higher dialect: ﴿Perhaps I may reach the means﴾ [Ghafir: 36], and a poet said in the other dialect:

*Verse:* "Show me a steed that died of emaciation, perhaps I [may] / see what you see, or a miserly, eternally [wealthy] one."

And God said: ﴿Oh, I wish I had been with them﴾ [al-Nisa: 73], and a poet said:

*Verse:* "Like the wish of Jabir when he said, 'Oh, if only I might encounter him / and spend some of my wealth.'"

As for *al-murīb* (the one who causes doubt), it means the one who causes suspicion and accusation. And "mercy" here is intended to mean prophethood.

God's words: ﴿So you increase me in nothing but loss﴾. *Takhsīr* means decrease.

Regarding the meaning of the statement there are two opinions:

One: "So you increase me in nothing but a clear perception of your own loss." This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. Al-Farraʾ said: the meaning is "so you increase me in nothing but loss *for you*," that is, whenever you offer me an excuse, it only increases your loss. Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: "nothing but loss *for you*, not for me." Some said: the meaning is "you increase me by what you have said only in attributing you to loss."

The second opinion: "So you increase me in nothing but ruin if I return to your religion." This is the meaning of Muqatil's statement.

If it is said: the apparent meaning of this is that he was in loss, and they increased his loss. We have already given the answer regarding His words: ﴿Had they gone out among you, they would have increased you in nothing but corruption﴾ [al-Tawba: 47].

God's words: ﴿This is the she-camel of God for you as a sign﴾. We have explained it in the surah of al-Aʿraf [73].

God's words: ﴿Enjoy yourselves in your homes﴾, that is: enjoy your lives. He expressed life by *tamattuʿ* (enjoyment), because the living are enjoying through the senses.

God's words: ﴿for three days﴾. The exegetes said: when the she-camel was hamstrung, her young went up the mountain and cried out three times. Salih said: "For every cry there is a term of one day. Indeed, on the first day your faces will become yellow, on the second day red, and on the third day black." When they awoke on the first day, their faces were yellow, so they shouted, wailed and wept, and knew it was the punishment. When they awoke on the second day, their faces were red, so they wailed and wept. When they awoke on the third day, their faces were black, as if they had been smeared with pitch, so they all cried out: "Surely the punishment has come upon you!" They prepared their shrouds and threw themselves on the ground, not knowing from where the punishment would come to them. When they awoke on the fourth day, a cry came to them from the sky containing the sound of every thunderbolt, and their hearts were torn apart within their chests. Muqatil said: they dug graves for themselves. When the sun rose on the fourth day and the punishment had not come to them, they thought God had had mercy on them, so they came out of their graves calling to one another, when Gabriel descended and stood above the city, blocking the light of the sun. When they saw him, they went back into their graves. He cried out to them with a shout: "Die where you are; the curse of God be upon you!" Their souls departed, their houses shook, and they fell upon their graves.

God's words: ﴿That is a promise﴾, that is: the punishment ﴿not to be denied﴾, that is: not a lie.

God's words: ﴿And from the disgrace of that day﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr and Ibn ʿAmir recited *yawmiʾidhin* with a kasra on the *mīm*. al-Kisaʾi recited it with a fatha on the *mīm* with the annexation (*iḍāfa*). Makki said: whoever puts a kasra on the *mīm* treats it as inflected and in the genitive, because *khizy* is annexed to the day, and does not make it indeclinable. Whoever puts a fatha, makes *al-yawm* indeclinable on the fatha, because it is annexed to something indeclinable, which is *idh* (when). Ibn Masʿud recited *wa-min khizyin* with tanwin and *yawmaʾidhin* with a fatha on the *mīm*. Ibn al-Anbari said: this *wāw* in His words *wa-min khizyin* is coordinated with an elided element, its estimated meaning being: "We saved them from the punishment and from the disgrace of that day." He said: it is also possible that it entered with a hidden verb, its interpretation being: "We saved Salih and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us, and We saved them from the disgrace of that day." He said: He only said *wa-akhadha* ("and seized") because the cry is taken to mean the shouting.

God's words: ﴿Oh, away with Thamud!﴾. They differed regarding the declension (*ṣarf*) of *Thamud* and its non-declension in five places: in (Hud: 69) ﴿Indeed, Thamud disbelieved in their Lord. Away with Thamud!﴾, in (al-Furqan: 38) ﴿and ʿAd and Thamud and the people of the well﴾, in (al-ʿAnkabut: 38) ﴿and ʿAd and Thamud, and it has become clear to you﴾, and in (al-Najm: 51) ﴿and Thamud, so He left none﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, Nafiʿ and Ibn ʿAmir recited with tanwin in four of these places, and left ﴿Away with Thamud!﴾ undeclined. Hamza recited these five words without declension, while al-Kisaʾi declined them all. It is reported from ʿAsim differently: Husayn al-Juʿfi reported from Abu Bakr from him that he declined the four words as Abu ʿAmr did. Yahya ibn Adam reported that he declined three: in (Hud: 69) "Indeed, Thamudan," and in (al-Furqan: 38) and (al-ʿAnkabut: 38). Hafs reported from him that he declined none of them, like Hamza.

Know that *Thamud* is sometimes meant as a tribe and sometimes meant as a clan (*ḥayy*). When it is meant as a tribe, it is not declined, and when it is meant as a clan, it is declined. As for what we have omitted, its explanation has already preceded [al-Aʿraf: 73, al-Tawba: 70] up to His words: ﴿And Our messengers came to Abraham﴾.

The messengers here are the angels. Regarding their number there are six opinions:

One: they were three: Gabriel, Michael and Israfil. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Said ibn Jubayr. Muqatil said: Gabriel, Michael and the Angel of Death. The second: they were twelve, also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas. The third: eight, said by Muhammad ibn Kaʿb. The fourth: nine, said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk. The fifth: eleven, said by al-Suddi. The sixth: four, related by al-Mawardi.

Regarding this good news there are four opinions:

One: it was the good news of a son, said by al-Hasan and Muqatil. The second: of the destruction of the people of Lot, said by Qatada. The third: of his prophethood, said by ʿIkrima. The fourth: that Muhammad would descend from his loins, mentioned by al-Mawardi.

God's words: ﴿They said, "Peace!"﴾. Ibn al-Anbari said: it is in the accusative by the verb of saying, because it is a quoted expression, and the second "peace" is in the nominative by an implied *ʿalaykum* ("upon you"). Al-Farraʾ said: in it there are two possibilities:

One: he implied *ʿalaykum* as the poet said:

*Verse:* "We said 'Peace,' so she shrank back from her governor, / and there was nothing but the flicking of the eyebrows."

The Arabs say: "We met and said: *salām, salām*."

The second: the people greeted him, but when he disapproved of them, he said: "*Salām*, who are you?" because he did not recognize them. Hamza and al-Kisaʾi recited *qāla silmun* ("he said, 'Peace'"), and it has the same meaning as *salām*, just as they say *ḥill* and *ḥalāl*, and *ḥirm* and *ḥarām*. In this case, the meaning of *silm* is "Peace be upon you." Abu ʿAli said: the meaning of the two readings is one, even though the wording differs. Al-Zajjaj said: whoever recites *silmun* means: "Our affair is peace," that is, there is no harm upon us.

God's words: ﴿Then he did not delay﴾, that is: he did not tarry until he brought a roasted calf, because he took them to be guests, and the angels had come to him in the form of handsome young men.

Regarding *ḥanīdh* (roasted meat) there are six opinions:

One: it is the well-cooked, said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and Qatada.

The second: it is that whose juice and fat drip while it is being roasted, said by Shammar ibn ʿAtiyya.

The third: it is what you dig in the earth and then cover over, which is a well-known practice of the people of the desert. Its origin is *maḥnūdh*, then it was called *ḥanīdh*, just as *ṭabīkh* is said for *maṭbūkh* and *qatīl* for *maqtūl*. This is the opinion of al-Farraʾ.

The fourth: it is roasted (*mashwī*), said by Abu ʿUbayda.

The fifth: roasted on heated stones, said by Muqatil and Ibn Qutayba.

The sixth: *samīṭ* (roasted whole), mentioned by al-Zajjaj, who said: it is said that it means only roasted, and it is said: roasted and dripping, and it is said: roasted on stones.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verse 70:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When he saw their hands not reaching towards it﴾, meaning the angels, ﴿not reaching towards it﴾, meaning the calf, ﴿he found them strange﴾, i.e., he disapproved of them. Abu 'Ubayda said: nakiruhum, ankarahum and istankarahum all mean the same. al-A'sha said:

؎ She disowned me, and what she disowned was nothing but the calamities of time: greying hair and baldness.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And he conceived fear of them﴾, i.e., he concealed fear within himself. al-Farra' said: It was a custom in their time that when people came to them and they brought them food but the guests did not touch it, they assumed they were enemies or thieves. Thereupon he conceived fear within himself, and they perceived that in his face, so they said: ﴿Fear not﴾.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, we have been sent to the people of Lot﴾. al-Zajjaj said: i.e., we have been sent with the punishment to them. Ibn al-Anbari said: The reason this is left implicit here is that the indication of it is present through God's mention of it in another surah.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 11, verses 71–72**

Allah's words: ﴿And his wife was standing﴾. Her name was Sarah. The scholars differed over where she was standing, giving three views:

The first: she was behind the curtain, listening to their conversation. This is reported from Wahb (ibn Munabbih).

The second: she was standing and serving them. This is reported from Mujahid and al-Suddi.

The third: she was standing and praying. This is reported from Muhammad ibn Ishaq.

(p. 130) Regarding His words ﴿so she laughed﴾, there are three views:

The first: laughing here means wondering (ta'ajjub). This is reported from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas.

The second: the meaning of "she laughed" is that she menstruated (haydh). This is reported from Mujahid and Ikrimah. Ibn Qutayba said: this is from their saying, "the hare laughed," when it menstruated. On this view, her menstruation at that time confirms the good news of a child, because one who does not menstruate does not conceive. Al-Farra' said: we have not heard from a trustworthy source that the meaning of "laughed" is "menstruated." Ibn al-Anbari said: al-Farra', Abu Ubayda and Abu Ubayd denied that "laughed" means "menstruated," but others recognised it. A poet said:

*The hyena laughs at the slain of Hudhayl,*
*while you see the wolf howling for them.*

Some philologists said: its meaning is "she menstruated."

The third: it is the well-known laughter, and this is the view of most scholars.

Regarding the cause of her laughter, there are six views:

The first: she laughed because of Abraham's intense fear of his guests, and she said: "Why does Abraham fear, when they are only three, and he is among his family and servants?" This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas, and Muqatil said the same.

The second: she laughed at the angels' good news to Abraham of a child. This is also reported from Ibn Abbas and Wahb ibn Munabbih. On this view she laughed out of joy at the good news, and there is inversion (taqdim and ta'khir) in the verse, meaning: "And his wife was standing, so We gave her good news, and she laughed." This is the view preferred by Ibn Qutayba.

(p. 131) The third: she laughed at the heedlessness of the people of Lut and the nearness of punishment to them. This is said by Qatada.

The fourth: she laughed at the guests' refusal to eat, and she said: "How strange are our guests! We serve them ourselves, and yet they do not eat our food!" This is said by al-Suddi.

The fifth: she laughed out of joy at being safe, because she had been afraid as Abraham had been. This is said by al-Farra'.

The sixth: she had said to Abraham: "Take your nephew Lut to you, for punishment will descend upon his people." When the angels came with their punishment, she laughed out of joy at having been right. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned this.

The scholars of tafsir said: Gabriel said to Sarah: "Rejoice, O laughing one, with a son named Ishaq, and after Ishaq, Ya'qub." They gave her the good news that she would bear Ishaq, and that she would live to see her grandson.

Regarding the meaning of *al-wara'* (behind/after), there are two views:

The first: it means "after." This is said by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas, preferred by Muqatil and Ibn Qutayba.

The second: *al-wara'* means the grandchild (walad al-walad). This is also reported from Ibn Abbas, and said by al-Sha'bi, and preferred by Abu Ubayda.

If it is asked: how can Ya'qub be "behind" Ishaq when he is his own son by blood, and "behind" means a grandchild? Ibn al-Anbari answered this, saying: the meaning is: "And from behind the one attributed to Ishaq, Ya'qub," because al-Wara' for Abraham was through Ishaq. Had He said, "And from behind, Ya'qub," it would not be known whether this *wara'* is attributed to Ishaq or to Isma'il. So it was attributed to Ishaq to make the meaning clear and remove the ambiguity. He said: it is also permissible for the child of Abraham who was not from Ishaq to be attributed to Sarah metaphorically, so the interpretation of the verse would be: "From behind the one attributed to Sarah and to Abraham through Ishaq, Ya'qub." Whoever takes *al-wara'* to mean "after" adheres to the apparent sense of the Arabic language.

The readers (qurra', i.e. the Qur'an reciters) differed over *Ya'qub*. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim read *Ya'qubu* with a *damma* (raf'). Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, and Hafs on the authority of 'Asim read *Ya'quba* with a *fatha* (nasb).

Al-Zajjaj said: there are two possibilities for the *raf'* of *Ya'qubu*:

One: it is a delayed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar), whose meaning is that it is placed first. The meaning is: "And Ya'qub will come to her from behind Ishaq."

Two: "And Ya'qub was established for her from behind Ishaq."

As for the one who reads it in the *nasb*, he takes it according to the meaning: the meaning is "We gave her Ishaq, and We gave her Ya'qub."

Allah's words: ﴿Woe to me! Shall I give birth while I am an old woman?﴾ This expression is said when announcing the arrival of a great matter. She did not intend it as a curse upon herself; it is simply a phrase that comes easily to women's tongues at a astonishing matter. Her words *a-alidu* ("shall I give birth") are an interrogative of wonder. Al-Zajjaj said: *shaykhan* ("old") is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). Ibn al-Anbari said: by these words she only meant to draw attention to her old age.

The scholars differed over the ages of Abraham and Sarah at that time, giving four views:

The first: Abraham was ninety-nine years old and Sarah was ninety-eight. This is said by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas.

The second: Abraham was one hundred years old and Sarah was ninety-nine. This is said by Mujahid.

(p. 133) The third: Abraham was ninety and Sarah was the same. This is said by Qatada.

The fourth: Abraham was one hundred and twenty years old and Sarah was ninety. This is said by 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr and Ibn Ishaq.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verse 73:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "Do you wonder at the decree of Allah?"﴾ That is, at His decree and His power, which is the bringing about of a child from between two elderly people. As-Suddi said: Sarah said to Jibril, "What is the sign of that?" So he took a dry stick in his hand and twisted it between his fingers, and it became green and moving, and she said, "Then He is indeed the one who slaughters for Allah" (dhabih, meaning a sacrifice offered to God).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you, O people of the house.﴾ In this there are two views:

The first: that it is a supplication from the angels for them.

The second: that it is a report of the establishment of that for them.

And among those blessings is the existence of most of the prophets and the tribes (al-asbat) from Ibrahim and Sarah.

Al-Hamid means al-mahmud (the one praised). As for al-Majid, Ibn Qutayba said: it means al-majid, who is the noble (al-sharif). Abu Sulayman al-Khattabi said: it is the one of vast generosity. The root of majd (glory) in their speech is breadth (al-si'ah); it is said, "a man is majid" when he is generous and of abundant giving. And in some proverbs: "In every tree there is fire, and al-markh and al-'afar have grown abundant (istamjada)," meaning: they have multiplied from it.

(p-134) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When the fear had left Abraham﴾, meaning the alarm that had afflicted him when they refused to eat. ﴿He began disputing with Us﴾. There is an ellipsis (idmar) here: "he began and started disputing with Us." What is meant is that he was disputing with Our messengers.

The exegetes (mufassirun) said: When they told him, ﴿We are about to destroy the people of this town﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 31], he said: "Will you destroy a town in which there are a hundred believers?" They said: "No." He said: "Will you destroy a town in which there are fifty believers?" They said: "No." He said: "Forty?" They said: "No." He kept reducing the number until he said: "One?" They said: "No." Then he said: ﴿Indeed, Lut is in it﴾, and they said: ﴿We know best who is in it﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 32]. This is the statement of Ibn Ishaq. Others said: It was said to him: "If there are five in it, We will not punish them," and there were in it none other than Lut and his two daughters. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: He said to them, "Will you destroy a town in which there are fourteen believers?" They said: "No." Abraham was counting them as fourteen, including Lut's wife, so he fell silent and his mind was at ease. In fact, they were thirteen, and they were destroyed.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed Abraham was forbearing, compassionate, and penitent﴾. We have explained this in (Bara'a: 114). At that point the messengers said to Abraham: ﴿O Abraham, turn away from this﴾, meaning the disputing. ﴿Indeed, the command of your Lord has come﴾ concerning their punishment. It was also said: The punishment of your Lord has come, so it cannot be turned back, because Allah has decreed it.

There is an ellipsis (idmar) here: "he began and started disputing with Us." What is meant is that he was disputing with Our messengers.

The exegetes (mufassirun) said: When they told him, ﴿We are about to destroy the people of this town﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 31], he said: "Will you destroy a town in which there are a hundred believers?" They said: "No." He said: "Will you destroy a town in which there are fifty believers?" They said: "No." He said: "Forty?" They said: "No." He kept reducing the number until he said: "One?" They said: "No." Then he said: ﴿Indeed, Lut is in it﴾, and they said: ﴿We know best who is in it﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 32]. This is the statement of Ibn Ishaq. Others said: It was said to him: "If there are five in it, We will not punish them," and there were in it none other than Lut and his two daughters.
