The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verses 77–81 (part 1 of 2):

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And when Our messengers came to Lut﴾. The exegetes (mufassirun) said: The angels departed from Ibrahim's presence toward the town of Lut, and they came to it in the evening. Al-Suddi related from his shaykhs: They came to it at midday. When they reached the river of Sodom (Sadum), they met Lut's daughter drawing water for her family. They said to her: "O girl, is there a lodging place?" She said: "Yes. Stay where you are and do not enter until I come to you," fearing for them from her people. Then she went to her father and said: "O my father, catch up with young men at the gate of the town. I have never seen faces more beautiful than theirs. Let not your people seize them and disgrace them." Now his people had forbidden him to host any man. So he brought them in and told no one of them except the household of Lut. But his wife went out and informed her people, and they came rushing toward him.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿He was distressed on their account﴾. Concerning this there are two views:
The first: his opinion of his people turned bad. This is said by Ibn 'Abbas.
The second: the arrival of the messengers distressed him, because he did not know them, and he feared for them from his people. This is said by Ibn Jarir.
Al-Zajjaj said: The origin of "sii'a bihim" (sīʾa bihim) is "suwiʾa bihim," from al-su' (evil). However, the waw was made quiescent and its kasra was transferred to the sin.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿and he felt constrained for them (wa-ḍāqa bihim dhar‘an)﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: He felt constrained (ḍāqa dhar‘an) on account of his guests. Al-Farra' said: The original form is "wa-ḍāqa dhar‘uhu bihim" (and his capacity was constrained by them). The verb was shifted from the dhar' (capacity) to the pronoun of Lut, and the dhar' was put in the accusative because the verb had been moved away from it, as in His saying: ﴿and the head glistens with grey hair﴾ [Maryam: 4]. Its meaning is: the greyness of the head glistened.
Al-Zajjaj said: It is said: "Fulan ḍāqa bi-amrihi dhar‘an" when he finds no way out from the unpleasant matter in that affair. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned three views concerning it:
The first: its meaning is that a great calamity befell him, to the extent that he could not ward it off from himself. So dhar' is a metaphor (kināya) for this meaning.
The second: its meaning is that his patience was constrained and the unpleasantness weighed heavily upon him. Its origin is from "dhara'a fulānan al-qay'" (vomit overcame someone), when it overpowers and outstrips him.
The third: the meaning is that his capacity (wus') was constrained by them, and dhar' and dhira' (forearm) stand in for wus' (capacity), because the dhira' is from the hand. The Arabs say: "This is not in my hand," meaning: "This is not within my capacity." What confirms this is that they put dhira' in the place of dhar', saying: "I was constrained by this matter by a forearm (ḍiqtu bihādhā al-amri dhirā‘an)." The poet said:
"To you, to you, (my capacity) was constrained by them, forearm-wise."
As for ʿaṣībun (ʿaṣīb), Abu 'Ubayda said: ʿaṣīb is the severe one who grips people with evil. He recited:
"A day of ʿaṣīb which grips the champions, / as the strong grips the long peace (salam)."
Abu 'Ubayd said: It is said "yawmun ʿaṣīb" and "yawmun ʿaṣabṣab" when it is severe.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿they came rushing toward him (yuhra‘ūna ilayhi)﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: "yuhra‘ūn" means they hasten. Al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i said: ihrā‘ (rushing) is not except hastening together with trembling. Ibn Qutayba said: ihrā‘ resembles trembling. It is said: "ahra‘a al-rajulu" when he hastened, in the form of the passive whose agent is not named, as it is said "urʿida" (he was made to tremble). Ibn al-Anbari said: ihrā‘ is a verb that falls upon the people, and it belongs to them in meaning, as the Arabs said: "qad ūlia al-rajulu bi-l-amr" (the man was made enamoured of the matter), so they made him the object, though he is the doer of the action. Similarly "urʿida Zayd" (Zayd was made to tremble) and "suhiya ʿAmr" (ʿAmr was made heedless) from al-sahw (forgetfulness). In each of these verbs, the noun came in the form of the object, although the estimated sense is that he is the doer of the verb, and no other doer is known for it. He said: Some grammarians said: It is not permissible to make the doer of the verb an object, and the doers of these mentioned verbs are omitted. The interpretation of "ūlia Zayd" is: his nature and disposition made him enamoured. "Urʿida al-rajul" means: his anger made him tremble. "Suhiya ʿAmr" means: his wealth or ignorance made him heedless. "Uhrii'a" means: his fear and terror made him rush. For this reason, these people formed these nouns in the manner of the object. He said: Some lexicographers said: ihrā‘ is only the hastening of one who is terrified and afraid. One is not called "muhra‘" (one rushed) for every hastener until panic and dread join his haste. The exegetes said: The cause of their rush was that Lut's wife had informed them about the guests.

﴿And before this (wa-min qablu)﴾, that is, before their coming to Lut, ﴿they used to do evil deeds (al-sayyi'āt)﴾, meaning their reprehensible act.

Concerning His words ﴿These are my daughters (hā’ulā’i banātī)﴾ there are two views:
The first: they were his daughters from his own loins. This is said by Ibn 'Abbas.
If it is asked: How did he use the plural when there were only two?
The answer: The plural may be used for two, as in His saying: ﴿and We were witnesses to their judgment﴾ [al-Anbiya': 78].
The second: he meant the women of his community (ummah), because every prophet is the father of his community. The meaning is that he offered them marriage, or ordered them to be content with their wives. This is the position of Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatada, and Ibn Jurayj.
If it is asked: How did he offer believing women to disbelievers? Concerning this there are two answers:
The first: such marriage was permissible in his law, and it was permissible at the beginning of Islam until it was abrogated (nusikha). This is said by al-Hasan.
The second: he offered them on condition that they embrace Islam. This is said by al-Zajjaj, and what confirms it is that offering them to them was contingent upon the contract of marriage, so it was permissible for it to be contingent upon another condition.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿They are purer for you (hunna aṭhharu lakum)﴾. Muqatil said: They are more lawful than having intercourse with men.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿So fear God (fa-ttaqū Allāh)﴾. Concerning this there are two views:
The first: fear His punishment. The second: fear His disobedience.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿and do not disgrace me regarding my guests (wa-lā tukhzūnī fī ḍayfī)﴾. Abu 'Amr and Nafi' vocalized the ya' of "ḍayfī" (with a short vowel). Concerning the meaning of this disgrace there are three views:
The first: it is disgrace (al-fadīḥa). This is said by Ibn 'Abbas.
The second: it is shame (al-istihyā'), and the meaning is: do not do to my guests an act which obliges me to feel shame, because the host is obliged to feel shame for every act that reaches his guest. The Arabs say: "Qad khazia al-rajul yakhzā khizāyatan" when he felt shame. The poet said:
"Of the white (women), she does not feel shame when the wind clings / her wrap to her, or when the jewelry slips from her neck."
The third: it means ruin (al-halāk), because the disgrace that falls upon the host in this situation obliges him to ruin. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned both.
Ibn Qutayba said: Here "ḍayf" is in the sense of "aḍyāf" (guests), and the singular indicates the plural, as you say: "These are my messenger and my agent (hā'ulā’i rasūlī wa-wakīlī)."

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Is there not among you a man who is rightly guided (rashīd)?﴾ Concerning what is intended by rashīd there are two views:
The first: a believer. The second: one who enjoins the good and forbids the evil. Both are related from Ibn 'Abbas.
Ibn al-Anbari said: It is permissible that rashīd means murshid (one who guides), so the meaning is: "Is there not among you a guide who admonishes you and makes known to you the ugliness of what you do?" Then rashīd is an attribute of the doer, like ʿalīm (knowing) and shahīd (witnessing). It is also permissible that rashīd means murshid in the sense of the one who is made rightly guided, so the meaning is: "Is there not among you a man whom God has made happy with the guidance He has granted him, who turns you away from committing this shame?" Then rashīd takes the place of the passive, like "al-kitāb al-ḥakīm" meaning "al-muḥkam" (the firmly-made book).

The words of the Exalted: ﴿You know we have no claim on your daughters (mā lanā fī banātika min ḥaqq)﴾. Concerning this there are two views:
The first: we have no need for them. This is said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.
The second: they are not wives for us, so that we would have a right to them. This is said by Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Qutayba.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And you surely know what we desire (wa-innaka la-ta‘lamu mā nurīd)﴾. 'Ata' said: "You surely know that we desire men, not women."

The words of the Exalted: ﴿If only I had power against you (law anna lī bikum quwwatan)﴾, that is, a group stronger than you by which I could prevail over you. It was said: By power he meant force (al-baṭsh). ﴿Or that I might take refuge in a strong pillar (aw āwī ilā rukn shadīd)﴾, that is, that I might join with a clan and a faction that would protect me. The answer to "law" is omitted, with the estimate: "I would have stood between you and disobedience." Abu 'Ubayda said: His saying "āwī" (take refuge) comes from their saying: "awaytu ilayka," so I take refuge (āwī ūiyyan), and the meaning is: I went to you and joined myself to you. The metaphorical sense of rukn (pillar) here is: the powerful, numerous, and protected clan. He recited:
"He takes refuge in a pillar among the pillars, / in a numerous host and a noble glory."
al-Ṭays means "much." It is said: "Atānā laban ṭays wa-sharāb ṭays," meaning: much.

They differed as to what time Lut said this. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that Lut had closed his door while the angels were with him in the house, and he was disputing with them and imploring them behind the door, while they were trying to force the door and sought to climb over the wall. When the angels saw the distress he was suffering, they said: "O Lut, we are messengers of your Lord. Open the door and leave us and them." So he opened the door and they entered. Jibril asked his Lord for permission to punish them, and He permitted him. So he struck their faces with his wing and blinded them. They withdrew saying: "Escape, escape! In the house of Lut are the most sorcerous people on earth!" They began to say: "O Lut, stay as you are until morning," threatening him. Lut said to them: "When is the time of their destruction?" They said: "The morning." He said: "If only you would destroy them now!" They said: "Is not the morning near?" Abu Salih related from Ibn 'Abbas: When they threatened him, he said to himself: "These people will leave me tomorrow, and I will remain with these (guests), and they will destroy me." So he said: "If only I had power against you."
I say: This applies only if we say that it was before he knew that they were angels. Others said: He only said this when they broke down his door and rushed upon him. Still others said: He said this when he forbade them from his guests and they refused.
In sum, by "rukn" he did not mean the support of God and His help, since he was never without that. He meant only the clan and the family.
Abu Hurayra related from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "May God have mercy on Lut; he used to take refuge in a strong pillar. God did not send any prophet after him except among a people of great kinship (tharwa) from his own people."

The words of the Exalted: ﴿They will never reach you (lan yaṣilū ilayka)﴾. Muqatil said: There is an implied element; its estimate is: "They will never reach you with evil." That is because they said to Lut: "We see with you men who have bewitched our eyes, so you will know tomorrow what you and your family will face." Then Jibril said to him: ﴿We are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you﴾.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿So travel with your family (fa-asri bi-ahlika)﴾. 'Asim, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i recited "fa-asri" with the hamza in pronunciation, from asraytu (I travelled by night). Ibn Kathir and Nafi' recited "fa-sri bi-ahlika" without a hamza, from saraytu (I travelled by night). Both are two dialects (lughatān). Al-Zajjaj said: It is said "saraytu" and "asraytu" when you travel at night. The poet said:
"I travelled with them until their mounts tired, / and even the fine horses, though not led by reins."
Al-Nabigha said:
"The Pleiades (al-Jawza') from which a sweeping (sāriya) wind swept over him, / driving the north wind upon him, a frozen hail."
They also related it as "saratā" (she travelled). As for "ahlika" (your family), Muqatil said: They are his wife and his two daughters, and the names of his two daughters were Ruthā and Zu'arathā. Al-Suddi said: The name of the elder was Rayya, and the name of the younger was ʿArūba, and by "his family" is meant his two daughters. As for "qiṭ‘" (a part), it is in the sense of "qiṭ‘a" (a portion). It is said: "Maḍā qiṭ‘un min al-layl," meaning: a portion of the night. Ibn 'Abbas said: By this he means: the last part of the night. Ibn Qutayba said: "bi-qiṭ‘" means: with a remnant that remains from its end. Ibn al-Anbari said: The mention of qiṭ‘ in the sense of qiṭ‘a is specific to the night, and one does not say: "ʿindī qiṭ‘un min al-thawb," meaning "I have a piece of the garment."

The words of the Exalted: ﴿and let none of you look back (wa-lā yaltafit minkum aḥad)﴾. Concerning this there are two views:
The first: it means: let none of you lag behind. This is said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.
The second: it is the well-known turning around (al-iltifāt), said by Mujahid and Muqatil.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verse 77–81 (part 2 of 2):

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿except your wife﴾. Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with the accusative on the ta' (ʾimraʾataka, with a fatha). Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Ibn Jammaz, from Abu Ja'far, read it with the nominative on the ta' (imraʾatuka, with a damma).

Al-Zajjaj said: Whoever reads with the accusative, the meaning is: "So set out with your family, except your wife." Whoever reads with the nominative, he takes it as referring to ﴿And let none of you look back, except your wife﴾. They were ordered to abandon looking back only so that they would not see the magnitude of the punishment that would descend upon them.

Ibn al-Anbari said this. On the reading with the nominative, the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), meaning: "But as for your wife, she will look back, and so there will befall her what befell them." When the exception is disjunctive, her looking back is an act of disobedience to her Lord, because He had recommended abandoning looking back.

Qatadah said: It was mentioned to us that she was with Lut when he left the town. When she heard the thunderous roar of the punishment, she looked back and said, "Oh, my people!" So a stone struck her and killed her. This is His saying: ﴿Indeed, what befalls them will befall her. Indeed, their appointed time is the morning﴾ for the punishment, ﴿the morning﴾.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Is not the morning near?﴾ The commentators said: The angels said, "Indeed their appointed time is the morning," and he (Lut) said, "I want it to be sooner than that." So they said to him: ﴿Is not the morning near?﴾

﴿And before this (wa-min qablu)﴾, that is, before their coming to Lut, ﴿they used to do evil deeds (al-sayyi'āt)﴾, meaning their reprehensible act.

If it is asked: How did he offer believing women to disbelievers? Concerning this there are two answers:
The first: such marriage was permissible in his law, and it was permissible at the beginning of Islam until it was abrogated (nusikha). This is said by al-Hasan.
The second: he offered them on condition that they embrace Islam. This is said by al-Zajjaj, and what confirms it is that offering them to them was contingent upon the contract of marriage, so it was permissible for it to be contingent upon another condition.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿They are purer for you (hunna aṭhharu lakum)﴾. Muqatil said: They are more lawful than having intercourse with men.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿So fear God (fa-ttaqū Allāh)﴾. Concerning this there are two views:
The first: fear His punishment. The second: fear His disobedience.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿and do not disgrace me regarding my guests (wa-lā tukhzūnī fī ḍayfī)﴾. Abu 'Amr and Nafi' vocalized the ya' of "ḍayfī" (with a short vowel). Concerning the meaning of this disgrace there are three views:
The first: it is disgrace (al-fadīḥa). This is said by Ibn 'Abbas.
The second: it is shame (al-istihyā'), and the meaning is: do not do to my guests an act which obliges me to feel shame, because the host is obliged to feel shame for every act that reaches his guest. The Arabs say: "Qad khazia al-rajul yakhzā khizāyatan" when he felt shame. The poet said:
"Of the white (women), she does not feel shame when the wind clings / her wrap to her, or when the jewelry slips from her neck."
The third: it means ruin (al-halāk), because the disgrace that falls upon the host in this situation obliges him to ruin. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned both.
Ibn Qutayba said: Here "ḍayf" is in the sense of "aḍyāf" (guests), and the singular indicates the plural, as you say: "These are my messenger and my agent (hā'ulā’i rasūlī wa-wakīlī)."

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Is there not among you a man who is rightly guided (rashīd)?﴾ Concerning what is intended by rashīd there are two views:
The first: a believer. The second: one who enjoins the good and forbids the evil. Both are related from Ibn 'Abbas.
Ibn al-Anbari said: It is permissible that rashīd means murshid (one who guides), so the meaning is: "Is there not among you a guide who admonishes you and makes known to you the ugliness of what you do?" Then rashīd is an attribute of the doer, like ʿalīm (knowing) and shahīd (witnessing). It is also permissible that rashīd means murshid in the sense of the one who is made rightly guided, so the meaning is: "Is there not among you a man whom God has made happy with the guidance He has granted him, who turns you away from committing this shame?" Then rashīd takes the place of the passive, like "al-kitāb al-ḥakīm" meaning "al-muḥkam" (the firmly-made book).

The words of the Exalted: ﴿You know we have no claim on your daughters (mā lanā fī banātika min ḥaqq)﴾. Concerning this there are two views:
The first: we have no need for them. This is said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.
The second: they are not wives for us, so that we would have a right to them. This is said by Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Qutayba.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And you surely know what we desire (wa-innaka la-ta‘lamu mā nurīd)﴾. 'Ata' said: "You surely know that we desire men, not women."

The words of the Exalted: ﴿If only I had power against you (law anna lī bikum quwwatan)﴾, that is, a group stronger than you by which I could prevail over you. It was said: By power he meant force (al-baṭsh). ﴿Or that I might take refuge in a strong pillar (aw āwī ilā rukn shadīd)﴾, that is, that I might join with a clan and a faction that would protect me. The answer to "law" is omitted, with the estimate: "I would have stood between you and disobedience." Abu 'Ubayda said: His saying "āwī" (take refuge) comes from their saying: "awaytu ilayka," so I take refuge (āwī ūiyyan), and the meaning is: I went to you and joined myself to you. The metaphorical sense of rukn (pillar) here is: the powerful, numerous, and protected clan. He recited:
"He takes refuge in a pillar among the pillars, / in a numerous host and a noble glory."
al-Ṭays means "much." It is said: "Atānā laban ṭays wa-sharāb ṭays," meaning: much.

They differed as to what time Lut said this. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that Lut had closed his door while the angels were with him in the house, and he was disputing with them and imploring them behind the door, while they were trying to force the door and sought to climb over the wall. When the angels saw the distress he was suffering, they said: "O Lut, we are messengers of your Lord. Open the door and leave us and them." So he opened the door and they entered. Jibril asked his Lord for permission to punish them, and He permitted him. So he struck their faces with his wing and blinded them. They withdrew saying: "Escape, escape! In the house of Lut are the most sorcerous people on earth!" They began to say: "O Lut, stay as you are until morning," threatening him. Lut said to them: "When is the time of their destruction?" They said: "The morning." He said: "If only you would destroy them now!" They said: "Is not the morning near?" Abu Salih related from Ibn 'Abbas: When they threatened him, he said to himself: "These people will leave me tomorrow, and I will remain with these (guests), and they will destroy me." So he said: "If only I had power against you."
I say: This applies only if we say that it was before he knew that they were angels. Others said: He only said this when they broke down his door and rushed upon him. Still others said: He said this when he forbade them from his guests and they refused.
In sum, by "rukn" he did not mean the support of God and His help, since he was never without that. He meant only the clan and the family.
Abu Hurayra related from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "May God have mercy on Lut; he used to take refuge in a strong pillar. God did not send any prophet after him except among a people of great kinship (tharwa) from his own people."

The words of the Exalted: ﴿They will never reach you (lan yaṣilū ilayka)﴾. Muqatil said: There is an implied element; its estimate is: "They will never reach you with evil." That is because they said to Lut: "We see with you men who have bewitched our eyes, so you will know tomorrow what you and your family will face." Then Jibril said to him: ﴿We are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you﴾.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿So travel with your family (fa-asri bi-ahlika)﴾. 'Asim, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i recited "fa-asri" with the hamza in pronunciation, from asraytu (I travelled by night). Ibn Kathir and Nafi' recited "fa-sri bi-ahlika" without a hamza, from saraytu (I travelled by night). Both are two dialects (lughatān). Al-Zajjaj said: It is said "saraytu" and "asraytu" when you travel at night. The poet said:
"I travelled with them until their mounts tired, / and even the fine horses, though not led by reins."
Al-Nabigha said:
"The Pleiades (al-Jawza') from which a sweeping (sāriya) wind swept over him, / driving the north wind upon him, a frozen hail."
They also related it as "saratā" (she travelled). As for "ahlika" (your family), Muqatil said: They are his wife and his two daughters, and the names of his two daughters were Ruthā and Zu'arathā. Al-Suddi said: The name of the elder was Rayya, and the name of the younger was ʿArūba, and by "his family" is meant his two daughters. As for "qiṭ‘" (a part), it is in the sense of "qiṭ‘a" (a portion). It is said: "Maḍā qiṭ‘un min al-layl," meaning: a portion of the night. Ibn 'Abbas said: By this he means: the last part of the night. Ibn Qutayba said: "bi-qiṭ‘" means: with a remnant that remains from its end. Ibn al-Anbari said: The mention of qiṭ‘ in the sense of qiṭ‘a is specific to the night, and one does not say: "ʿindī qiṭ‘un min al-thawb," meaning "I have a piece of the garment."

The words of the Exalted: ﴿and let none of you look back (wa-lā yaltafit minkum aḥad)﴾. Concerning this there are two views:
The first: it means: let none of you lag behind. This is said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.
The second: it is the well-known turning around (al-iltifāt), said by Mujahid and Muqatil.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verse 77–81 (part 2 of 2):

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿except your wife﴾. Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with the accusative on the ta' (ʾimraʾataka, with a fatha). Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Ibn Jammaz, from Abu Ja'far, read it with the nominative on the ta' (imraʾatuka, with a damma).

Al-Zajjaj said: Whoever reads with the accusative, the meaning is: "So set out with your family, except your wife." Whoever reads with the nominative, he takes it as referring to ﴿And let none of you look back, except your wife﴾. They were ordered to abandon looking back only so that they would not see the magnitude of the punishment that would descend upon them.

Ibn al-Anbari said this. On the reading with the nominative, the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), meaning: "But as for your wife, she will look back, and so there will befall her what befell them." When the exception is disjunctive, her looking back is an act of disobedience to her Lord, because He had recommended abandoning looking back.

Qatadah said: It was mentioned to us that she was with Lut when he left the town. When she heard the thunderous roar of the punishment, she looked back and said, "Oh, my people!" So a stone struck her and killed her. This is His saying: ﴿Indeed, what befalls them will befall her. Indeed, their appointed time is the morning﴾ for the punishment, ﴿the morning﴾.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Is not the morning near?﴾ The commentators said: The angels said, "Indeed their appointed time is the morning," and he (Lut) said, "I want it to be sooner than that." So they said to him: ﴿Is not the morning near?﴾

The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verses 77–81 (part 1 of 2):

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And when Our messengers came to Lut﴾. The exegetes (mufassirun) said: The angels departed from Ibrahim's presence toward the town of Lut, and they came to it in the evening. Al-Suddi related from his shaykhs: They came to it at midday. When they reached the river of Sodom (Sadum), they met Lut's daughter drawing water for her family. They said to her: "O girl, is there a lodging place?" She said: "Yes. Stay where you are and do not enter until I come to you," fearing for them from her people. Then she went to her father and said: "O my father, catch up with young men at the gate of the town. I have never seen faces more beautiful than theirs. Let not your people seize them and disgrace them." Now his people had forbidden him to host any man. So he brought them in and told no one of them except the household of Lut. But his wife went out and informed her people, and they came rushing toward him.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿He was distressed on their account﴾. Concerning this there are two views:
The first: his opinion of his people turned bad. This is said by Ibn 'Abbas.
The second: the arrival of the messengers distressed him, because he did not know them, and he feared for them from his people. This is said by Ibn Jarir.
Al-Zajjaj said: The origin of "sii'a bihim" (sīʾa bihim) is "suwiʾa bihim," from al-su' (evil). However, the waw was made quiescent and its kasra was transferred to the sin.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿and he felt constrained for them (wa-ḍāqa bihim dhar‘an)﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: He felt constrained (ḍāqa dhar‘an) on account of his guests. Al-Farra' said: The original form is "wa-ḍāqa dhar‘uhu bihim" (and his capacity was constrained by them). The verb was shifted from the dhar' (capacity) to the pronoun of Lut, and the dhar' was put in the accusative because the verb had been moved away from it, as in His saying: ﴿and the head glistens with grey hair﴾ [Maryam: 4]. Its meaning is: the greyness of the head glistened.
Al-Zajjaj said: It is said: "Fulan ḍāqa bi-amrihi dhar‘an" when he finds no way out from the unpleasant matter in that affair. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned three views concerning it:
The first: its meaning is that a great calamity befell him, to the extent that he could not ward it off from himself. So dhar' is a metaphor (kināya) for this meaning.
The second: its meaning is that his patience was constrained and the unpleasantness weighed heavily upon him. Its origin is from "dhara'a fulānan al-qay'" (vomit overcame someone), when it overpowers and outstrips him.
The third: the meaning is that his capacity (wus') was constrained by them, and dhar' and dhira' (forearm) stand in for wus' (capacity), because the dhira' is from the hand. The Arabs say: "This is not in my hand," meaning: "This is not within my capacity." What confirms this is that they put dhira' in the place of dhar', saying: "I was constrained by this matter by a forearm (ḍiqtu bihādhā al-amri dhirā‘an)." The poet said:
"To you, to you, (my capacity) was constrained by them, forearm-wise."
As for ʿaṣībun (ʿaṣīb), Abu 'Ubayda said: ʿaṣīb is the severe one who grips people with evil. He recited:
"A day of ʿaṣīb which grips the champions, / as the strong grips the long peace (salam)."
Abu 'Ubayd said: It is said "yawmun ʿaṣīb" and "yawmun ʿaṣabṣab" when it is severe.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿they came rushing toward him (yuhra‘ūna ilayhi)﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: "yuhra‘ūn" means they hasten. Al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i said: ihrā‘ (rushing) is not except hastening together with trembling. Ibn Qutayba said: ihrā‘ resembles trembling. It is said: "ahra‘a al-rajulu" when he hastened, in the form of the passive whose agent is not named, as it is said "urʿida" (he was made to tremble). Ibn al-Anbari said: ihrā‘ is a verb that falls upon the people, and it belongs to them in meaning, as the Arabs said: "qad ūlia al-rajulu bi-l-amr" (the man was made enamoured of the matter), so they made him the object, though he is the doer of the action. Similarly "urʿida Zayd" (Zayd was made to tremble) and "suhiya ʿAmr" (ʿAmr was made heedless) from al-sahw (forgetfulness). In each of these verbs, the noun came in the form of the object, although the estimated sense is that he is the doer of the verb, and no other doer is known for it. He said: Some grammarians said: It is not permissible to make the doer of the verb an object, and the doers of these mentioned verbs are omitted. The interpretation of "ūlia Zayd" is: his nature and disposition made him enamoured. "Urʿida al-rajul" means: his anger made him tremble. "Suhiya ʿAmr" means: his wealth or ignorance made him heedless. "Uhrii'a" means: his fear and terror made him rush. For this reason, these people formed these nouns in the manner of the object. He said: Some lexicographers said: ihrā‘ is only the hastening of one who is terrified and afraid. One is not called "muhra‘" (one rushed) for every hastener until panic and dread join his haste. The exegetes said: The cause of their rush was that Lut's wife had informed them about the guests.

﴿And before this (wa-min qablu)﴾, that is, before their coming to Lut, ﴿they used to do evil deeds (al-sayyi'āt)﴾, meaning their reprehensible act.

Concerning His words ﴿These are my daughters (hā’ulā’i banātī)﴾ there are two views:
The first: they were his daughters from his own loins. This is said by Ibn 'Abbas.
If it is asked: How did he use the plural when there were only two?
The answer: The plural may be used for two, as in His saying: ﴿and We were witnesses to their judgment﴾ [al-Anbiya': 78].
The second: he meant the women of his community (ummah), because every prophet is the father of his community. The meaning is that he offered them marriage, or ordered them to be content with their wives. This is the position of Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatada, and Ibn Jurayj.
If it is asked: How did he offer believing women to disbelievers? Concerning this there are two answers:
The first: such marriage was permissible in his law, and it was permissible at the beginning of Islam until it was abrogated (nusikha). This is said by al-Hasan.
The second: he offered them on condition that they embrace Islam. This is said by al-Zajjaj, and what confirms it is that offering them to them was contingent upon the contract of marriage, so it was permissible for it to be contingent upon another condition.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿They are purer for you (hunna aṭhharu lakum)﴾. Muqatil said: They are more lawful than having intercourse with men.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿So fear God (fa-ttaqū Allāh)﴾. Concerning this there are two views:
The first: fear His punishment. The second: fear His disobedience.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿and do not disgrace me regarding my guests (wa-lā tukhzūnī fī ḍayfī)﴾. Abu 'Amr and Nafi' vocalized the ya' of "ḍayfī" (with a short vowel). Concerning the meaning of this disgrace there are three views:
The first: it is disgrace (al-fadīḥa). This is said by Ibn 'Abbas.
The second: it is shame (al-istihyā'), and the meaning is: do not do to my guests an act which obliges me to feel shame, because the host is obliged to feel shame for every act that reaches his guest. The Arabs say: "Qad khazia al-rajul yakhzā khizāyatan" when he felt shame. The poet said:
"Of the white (women), she does not feel shame when the wind clings / her wrap to her, or when the jewelry slips from her neck."
The third: it means ruin (al-halāk), because the disgrace that falls upon the host in this situation obliges him to ruin. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned both.
Ibn Qutayba said: Here "ḍayf" is in the sense of "aḍyāf" (guests), and the singular indicates the plural, as you say: "These are my messenger and my agent (hā'ulā’i rasūlī wa-wakīlī)."

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Is there not among you a man who is rightly guided (rashīd)?﴾ Concerning what is intended by rashīd there are two views:
The first: a believer. The second: one who enjoins the good and forbids the evil. Both are related from Ibn 'Abbas.
Ibn al-Anbari said: It is permissible that rashīd means murshid (one who guides), so the meaning is: "Is there not among you a guide who admonishes you and makes known to you the ugliness of what you do?" Then rashīd is an attribute of the doer, like ʿalīm (knowing) and shahīd (witnessing). It is also permissible that rashīd means murshid in the sense of the one who is made rightly guided, so the meaning is: "Is there not among you a man whom God has made happy with the guidance He has granted him, who turns you away from committing this shame?" Then rashīd takes the place of the passive, like "al-kitāb al-ḥakīm" meaning "al-muḥkam" (the firmly-made book).

The words of the Exalted: ﴿You know we have no claim on your daughters (mā lanā fī banātika min ḥaqq)﴾. Concerning this there are two views:
The first: we have no need for them. This is said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.
The second: they are not wives for us, so that we would have a right to them. This is said by Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Qutayba.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And you surely know what we desire (wa-innaka la-ta‘lamu mā nurīd)﴾. 'Ata' said: "You surely know that we desire men, not women."

The words of the Exalted: ﴿If only I had power against you (law anna lī bikum quwwatan)﴾, that is, a group stronger than you by which I could prevail over you. It was said: By power he meant force (al-baṭsh). ﴿Or that I might take refuge in a strong pillar (aw āwī ilā rukn shadīd)﴾, that is, that I might join with a clan and a faction that would protect me. The answer to "law" is omitted, with the estimate: "I would have stood between you and disobedience." Abu 'Ubayda said: His saying "āwī" (take refuge) comes from their saying: "awaytu ilayka," so I take refuge (āwī ūiyyan), and the meaning is: I went to you and joined myself to you. The metaphorical sense of rukn (pillar) here is: the powerful, numerous, and protected clan. He recited:
"He takes refuge in a pillar among the pillars, / in a numerous host and a noble glory."
al-Ṭays means "much." It is said: "Atānā laban ṭays wa-sharāb ṭays," meaning: much.

They differed as to what time Lut said this. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that Lut had closed his door while the angels were with him in the house, and he was disputing with them and imploring them behind the door, while they were trying to force the door and sought to climb over the wall. When the angels saw the distress he was suffering, they said: "O Lut, we are messengers of your Lord. Open the door and leave us and them." So he opened the door and they entered. Jibril asked his Lord for permission to punish them, and He permitted him. So he struck their faces with his wing and blinded them. They withdrew saying: "Escape, escape! In the house of Lut are the most sorcerous people on earth!" They began to say: "O Lut, stay as you are until morning," threatening him. Lut said to them: "When is the time of their destruction?" They said: "The morning." He said: "If only you would destroy them now!" They said: "Is not the morning near?" Abu Salih related from Ibn 'Abbas: When they threatened him, he said to himself: "These people will leave me tomorrow, and I will remain with these (guests), and they will destroy me." So he said: "If only I had power against you."
I say: This applies only if we say that it was before he knew that they were angels. Others said: He only said this when they broke down his door and rushed upon him. Still others said: He said this when he forbade them from his guests and they refused.
In sum, by "rukn" he did not mean the support of God and His help, since he was never without that. He meant only the clan and the family.
Abu Hurayra related from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "May God have mercy on Lut; he used to take refuge in a strong pillar. God did not send any prophet after him except among a people of great kinship (tharwa) from his own people."

The words of the Exalted: ﴿They will never reach you (lan yaṣilū ilayka)﴾. Muqatil said: There is an implied element; its estimate is: "They will never reach you with evil." That is because they said to Lut: "We see with you men who have bewitched our eyes, so you will know tomorrow what you and your family will face." Then Jibril said to him: ﴿We are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you﴾.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿So travel with your family (fa-asri bi-ahlika)﴾. 'Asim, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i recited "fa-asri" with the hamza in pronunciation, from asraytu (I travelled by night). Ibn Kathir and Nafi' recited "fa-sri bi-ahlika" without a hamza, from saraytu (I travelled by night). Both are two dialects (lughatān). Al-Zajjaj said: It is said "saraytu" and "asraytu" when you travel at night. The poet said:
"I travelled with them until their mounts tired, / and even the fine horses, though not led by reins."
Al-Nabigha said:
"The Pleiades (al-Jawza') from which a sweeping (sāriya) wind swept over him, / driving the north wind upon him, a frozen hail."
They also related it as "saratā" (she travelled). As for "ahlika" (your family), Muqatil said: They are his wife and his two daughters, and the names of his two daughters were Ruthā and Zu'arathā. Al-Suddi said: The name of the elder was Rayya, and the name of the younger was ʿArūba, and by "his family" is meant his two daughters. As for "qiṭ‘" (a part), it is in the sense of "qiṭ‘a" (a portion). It is said: "Maḍā qiṭ‘un min al-layl," meaning: a portion of the night. Ibn 'Abbas said: By this he means: the last part of the night. Ibn Qutayba said: "bi-qiṭ‘" means: with a remnant that remains from its end. Ibn al-Anbari said: The mention of qiṭ‘ in the sense of qiṭ‘a is specific to the night, and one does not say: "ʿindī qiṭ‘un min al-thawb," meaning "I have a piece of the garment."

The words of the Exalted: ﴿and let none of you look back (wa-lā yaltafit minkum aḥad)﴾. Concerning this there are two views:
The first: it means: let none of you lag behind. This is said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.
The second: it is the well-known turning around (al-iltifāt), said by Mujahid and Muqatil.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verse 77–81 (part 2 of 2):

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿except your wife﴾. Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with the accusative on the ta' (ʾimraʾataka, with a fatha). Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Ibn Jammaz, from Abu Ja'far, read it with the nominative on the ta' (imraʾatuka, with a damma).

Al-Zajjaj said: Whoever reads with the accusative, the meaning is: "So set out with your family, except your wife." Whoever reads with the nominative, he takes it as referring to ﴿And let none of you look back, except your wife﴾. They were ordered to abandon looking back only so that they would not see the magnitude of the punishment that would descend upon them.

Ibn al-Anbari said this. On the reading with the nominative, the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), meaning: "But as for your wife, she will look back, and so there will befall her what befell them." When the exception is disjunctive, her looking back is an act of disobedience to her Lord, because He had recommended abandoning looking back.

Qatadah said: It was mentioned to us that she was with Lut when he left the town. When she heard the thunderous roar of the punishment, she looked back and said, "Oh, my people!" So a stone struck her and killed her. This is His saying: ﴿Indeed, what befalls them will befall her. Indeed, their appointed time is the morning﴾ for the punishment, ﴿the morning﴾.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Is not the morning near?﴾ The commentators said: The angels said, "Indeed their appointed time is the morning," and he (Lut) said, "I want it to be sooner than that." So they said to him: ﴿Is not the morning near?﴾

The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verses 77–81 (part 1 of 2):

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And when Our messengers came to Lut﴾. The exegetes (mufassirun) said: The angels departed from Ibrahim's presence toward the town of Lut, and they came to it in the evening. Al-Suddi related from his shaykhs: They came to it at midday. When they reached the river of Sodom (Sadum), they met Lut's daughter drawing water for her family. They said to her: "O girl, is there a lodging place?" She said: "Yes. Stay where you are and do not enter until I come to you," fearing for them from her people. Then she went to her father and said: "O my father, catch up with young men at the gate of the town. I have never seen faces more beautiful than theirs. Let not your people seize them and disgrace them." Now his people had forbidden him to host any man. So he brought them in and told no one of them except the household of Lut. But his wife went out and informed her people, and they came rushing toward him.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿He was distressed on their account﴾. Concerning this there are two views:
The first: his opinion of his people turned bad. This is said by Ibn 'Abbas.
The second: the arrival of the messengers distressed him, because he did not know them, and he feared for them from his people. This is said by Ibn Jarir.
Al-Zajjaj said: The origin of "sii'a bihim" (sīʾa bihim) is "suwiʾa bihim," from al-su' (evil). However, the waw was made quiescent and its kasra was transferred to the sin.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿and he felt constrained for them (wa-ḍāqa bihim dhar‘an)﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: He felt constrained (ḍāqa dhar‘an) on account of his guests. Al-Farra' said: The original form is "wa-ḍāqa dhar‘uhu bihim" (and his capacity was constrained by them). The verb was shifted from the dhar' (capacity) to the pronoun of Lut, and the dhar' was put in the accusative because the verb had been moved away from it, as in His saying: ﴿and the head glistens with grey hair﴾ [Maryam: 4]. Its meaning is: the greyness of the head glistened.
Al-Zajjaj said: It is said: "Fulan ḍāqa bi-amrihi dhar‘an" when he finds no way out from the unpleasant matter in that affair. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned three views concerning it:
The first: its meaning is that a great calamity befell him, to the extent that he could not ward it off from himself. So dhar' is a metaphor (kināya) for this meaning.
The second: its meaning is that his patience was constrained and the unpleasantness weighed heavily upon him. Its origin is from "dhara'a fulānan al-qay'" (vomit overcame someone), when it overpowers and outstrips him.
The third: the meaning is that his capacity (wus') was constrained by them, and dhar' and dhira' (forearm) stand in for wus' (capacity), because the dhira' is from the hand. The Arabs say: "This is not in my hand," meaning: "This is not within my capacity." What confirms this is that they put dhira' in the place of dhar', saying: "I was constrained by this matter by a forearm (ḍiqtu bihādhā al-amri dhirā‘an)." The poet said:
"To you, to you, (my capacity) was constrained by them, forearm-wise."
As for ʿaṣībun (ʿaṣīb), Abu 'Ubayda said: ʿaṣīb is the severe one who grips people with evil. He recited:
"A day of ʿaṣīb which grips the champions, / as the strong grips the long peace (salam)."
Abu 'Ubayd said: It is said "yawmun ʿaṣīb" and "yawmun ʿaṣabṣab" when it is severe.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿they came rushing toward him (yuhra‘ūna ilayhi)﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: "yuhra‘ūn" means they hasten. Al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i said: ihrā‘ (rushing) is not except hastening together with trembling. Ibn Qutayba said: ihrā‘ resembles trembling. It is said: "ahra‘a al-rajulu" when he hastened, in the form of the passive whose agent is not named, as it is said "urʿida" (he was made to tremble). Ibn al-Anbari said: ihrā‘ is a verb that falls upon the people, and it belongs to them in meaning, as the Arabs said: "qad ūlia al-rajulu bi-l-amr" (the man was made enamoured of the matter), so they made him the object, though he is the doer of the action. Similarly "urʿida Zayd" (Zayd was made to tremble) and "suhiya ʿAmr" (ʿAmr was made heedless) from al-sahw (forgetfulness). In each of these verbs, the noun came in the form of the object, although the estimated sense is that he is the doer of the verb, and no other doer is known for it. He said: Some grammarians said: It is not permissible to make the doer of the verb an object, and the doers of these mentioned verbs are omitted. The interpretation of "ūlia Zayd" is: his nature and disposition made him enamoured. "Urʿida al-rajul" means: his anger made him tremble. "Suhiya ʿAmr" means: his wealth or ignorance made him heedless. "Uhrii'a" means: his fear and terror made him rush. For this reason, these people formed these nouns in the manner of the object. He said: Some lexicographers said: ihrā‘ is only the hastening of one who is terrified and afraid. One is not called "muhra‘" (one rushed) for every hastener until panic and dread join his haste. The exegetes said: The cause of their rush was that Lut's wife had informed them about the guests.

﴿And before this (wa-min qablu)﴾, that is, before their coming to Lut, ﴿they used to do evil deeds (al-sayyi'āt)﴾, meaning their reprehensible act.

Concerning His words ﴿These are my daughters (hā’ulā’i banātī)﴾ there are two views:
The first: they were his daughters from his own loins. This is said by Ibn 'Abbas.
If it is asked: How did he use the plural when there were only two?
The answer: The plural may be used for two, as in His saying: ﴿and We were witnesses to their judgment﴾ [al-Anbiya': 78].
The second: he meant the women of his community (ummah), because every prophet is the father of his community. The meaning is that he offered them marriage, or ordered them to be content with their wives. This is the position of Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatada, and Ibn Jurayj.
If it is asked: How did he offer believing women to disbelievers? Concerning this there are two answers:
The first: such marriage was permissible in his law, and it was permissible at the beginning of Islam until it was abrogated (nusikha). This is said by al-Hasan.
The second: he offered them on condition that they embrace Islam. This is said by al-Zajjaj, and what confirms it is that offering them to them was contingent upon the contract of marriage, so it was permissible for it to be contingent upon another condition.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿They are purer for you (hunna aṭhharu lakum)﴾. Muqatil said: They are more lawful than having intercourse with men.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿So fear God (fa-ttaqū Allāh)﴾. Concerning this there are two views:
The first: fear His punishment. The second: fear His disobedience.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿and do not disgrace me regarding my guests (wa-lā tukhzūnī fī ḍayfī)﴾. Abu 'Amr and Nafi' vocalized the ya' of "ḍayfī" (with a short vowel). Concerning the meaning of this disgrace there are three views:
The first: it is disgrace (al-fadīḥa). This is said by Ibn 'Abbas.
The second: it is shame (al-istihyā'), and the meaning is: do not do to my guests an act which obliges me to feel shame, because the host is obliged to feel shame for every act that reaches his guest. The Arabs say: "Qad khazia al-rajul yakhzā khizāyatan" when he felt shame. The poet said:
"Of the white (women), she does not feel shame when the wind clings / her wrap to her, or when the jewelry slips from her neck."
The third: it means ruin (al-halāk), because the disgrace that falls upon the host in this situation obliges him to ruin. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned both.
Ibn Qutayba said: Here "ḍayf" is in the sense of "aḍyāf" (guests), and the singular indicates the plural, as you say: "These are my messenger and my agent (hā'ulā’i rasūlī wa-wakīlī)."

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Is there not among you a man who is rightly guided (rashīd)?﴾ Concerning what is intended by rashīd there are two views:
The first: a believer. The second: one who enjoins the good and forbids the evil. Both are related from Ibn 'Abbas.
Ibn al-Anbari said: It is permissible that rashīd means murshid (one who guides), so the meaning is: "Is there not among you a guide who admonishes you and makes known to you the ugliness of what you do?" Then rashīd is an attribute of the doer, like ʿalīm (knowing) and shahīd (witnessing). It is also permissible that rashīd means murshid in the sense of the one who is made rightly guided, so the meaning is: "Is there not among you a man whom God has made happy with the guidance He has granted him, who turns you away from committing this shame?" Then rashīd takes the place of the passive, like "al-kitāb al-ḥakīm" meaning "al-muḥkam" (the firmly-made book).

The words of the Exalted: ﴿You know we have no claim on your daughters (mā lanā fī banātika min ḥaqq)﴾. Concerning this there are two views:
The first: we have no need for them. This is said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.
The second: they are not wives for us, so that we would have a right to them. This is said by Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Qutayba.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And you surely know what we desire (wa-innaka la-ta‘lamu mā nurīd)﴾. 'Ata' said: "You surely know that we desire men, not women."

The words of the Exalted: ﴿If only I had power against you (law anna lī bikum quwwatan)﴾, that is, a group stronger than you by which I could prevail over you. It was said: By power he meant force (al-baṭsh). ﴿Or that I might take refuge in a strong pillar (aw āwī ilā rukn shadīd)﴾, that is, that I might join with a clan and a faction that would protect me. The answer to "law" is omitted, with the estimate: "I would have stood between you and disobedience." Abu 'Ubayda said: His saying "āwī" (take refuge) comes from their saying: "awaytu ilayka," so I take refuge (āwī ūiyyan), and the meaning is: I went to you and joined myself to you. The metaphorical sense of rukn (pillar) here is: the powerful, numerous, and protected clan. He recited:
"He takes refuge in a pillar among the pillars, / in a numerous host and a noble glory."
al-Ṭays means "much." It is said: "Atānā laban ṭays wa-sharāb ṭays," meaning: much.

They differed as to what time Lut said this. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that Lut had closed his door while the angels were with him in the house, and he was disputing with them and imploring them behind the door, while they were trying to force the door and sought to climb over the wall. When the angels saw the distress he was suffering, they said: "O Lut, we are messengers of your Lord. Open the door and leave us and them." So he opened the door and they entered. Jibril asked his Lord for permission to punish them, and He permitted him. So he struck their faces with his wing and blinded them. They withdrew saying: "Escape, escape! In the house of Lut are the most sorcerous people on earth!" They began to say: "O Lut, stay as you are until morning," threatening him. Lut said to them: "When is the time of their destruction?" They said: "The morning." He said: "If only you would destroy them now!" They said: "Is not the morning near?" Abu Salih related from Ibn 'Abbas: When they threatened him, he said to himself: "These people will leave me tomorrow, and I will remain with these (guests), and they will destroy me." So he said: "If only I had power against you."
I say: This applies only if we say that it was before he knew that they were angels. Others said: He only said this when they broke down his door and rushed upon him. Still others said: He said this when he forbade them from his guests and they refused.
In sum, by "rukn" he did not mean the support of God and His help, since he was never without that. He meant only the clan and the family.
Abu Hurayra related from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "May God have mercy on Lut; he used to take refuge in a strong pillar. God did not send any prophet after him except among a people of great kinship (tharwa) from his own people."

The words of the Exalted: ﴿They will never reach you (lan yaṣilū ilayka)﴾. Muqatil said: There is an implied element; its estimate is: "They will never reach you with evil." That is because they said to Lut: "We see with you men who have bewitched our eyes, so you will know tomorrow what you and your family will face." Then Jibril said to him: ﴿We are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you﴾.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿So travel with your family (fa-asri bi-ahlika)﴾. 'Asim, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i recited "fa-asri" with the hamza in pronunciation, from asraytu (I travelled by night). Ibn Kathir and Nafi' recited "fa-sri bi-ahlika" without a hamza, from saraytu (I travelled by night). Both are two dialects (lughatān). Al-Zajjaj said: It is said "saraytu" and "asraytu" when you travel at night. The poet said:
"I travelled with them until their mounts tired, / and even the fine horses, though not led by reins."
Al-Nabigha said:
"The Pleiades (al-Jawza') from which a sweeping (sāriya) wind swept over him, / driving the north wind upon him, a frozen hail."
They also related it as "saratā" (she travelled). As for "ahlika" (your family), Muqatil said: They are his wife and his two daughters, and the names of his two daughters were Ruthā and Zu'arathā. Al-Suddi said: The name of the elder was Rayya, and the name of the younger was ʿArūba, and by "his family" is meant his two daughters. As for "qiṭ‘" (a part), it is in the sense of "qiṭ‘a" (a portion). It is said: "Maḍā qiṭ‘un min al-layl," meaning: a portion of the night. Ibn 'Abbas said: By this he means: the last part of the night. Ibn Qutayba said: "bi-qiṭ‘" means: with a remnant that remains from its end. Ibn al-Anbari said: The mention of qiṭ‘ in the sense of qiṭ‘a is specific to the night, and one does not say: "ʿindī qiṭ‘un min al-thawb," meaning "I have a piece of the garment."

The words of the Exalted: ﴿and let none of you look back (wa-lā yaltafit minkum aḥad)﴾. Concerning this there are two views:
The first: it means: let none of you lag behind. This is said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.
The second: it is the well-known turning around (al-iltifāt), said by Mujahid and Muqatil.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verse 77–81 (part 2 of 2):

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿except your wife﴾. Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with the accusative on the ta' (ʾimraʾataka, with a fatha). Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Ibn Jammaz, from Abu Ja'far, read it with the nominative on the ta' (imraʾatuka, with a damma).

Al-Zajjaj said: Whoever reads with the accusative, the meaning is: "So set out with your family, except your wife." Whoever reads with the nominative, he takes it as referring to ﴿And let none of you look back, except your wife﴾. They were ordered to abandon looking back only so that they would not see the magnitude of the punishment that would descend upon them.

Ibn al-Anbari said this. On the reading with the nominative, the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), meaning: "But as for your wife, she will look back, and so there will befall her what befell them." When the exception is disjunctive, her looking back is an act of disobedience to her Lord, because He had recommended abandoning looking back.

Qatadah said: It was mentioned to us that she was with Lut when he left the town. When she heard the thunderous roar of the punishment, she looked back and said, "Oh, my people!" So a stone struck her and killed her. This is His saying: ﴿Indeed, what befalls them will befall her. Indeed, their appointed time is the morning﴾ for the punishment, ﴿the morning﴾.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Is not the morning near?﴾ The commentators said: The angels said, "Indeed their appointed time is the morning," and he (Lut) said, "I want it to be sooner than that." So they said to him: ﴿Is not the morning near?﴾

The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verses 77–81 (part 1 of 2):

The first: its meaning is that a great calamity befell him, to the extent that he could not ward it off from himself. So dhar' is a metaphor (kināya) for this meaning.
The second: its meaning is that his patience was constrained and the unpleasantness weighed heavily upon him. Its origin is from "dhara'a fulānan al-qay'" (vomit overcame someone), when it overpowers and outstrips him.
The third: the meaning is that his capacity (wus') was constrained by them, and dhar' and dhira' (forearm) stand in for wus' (capacity), because the dhira' is from the hand. The Arabs say: "This is not in my hand," meaning: "This is not within my capacity." What confirms this is that they put dhira' in the place of dhar', saying: "I was constrained by this matter by a forearm (ḍiqtu bihādhā al-amri dhirā‘an)." The poet said:
"To you, to you, (my capacity) was constrained by them, forearm-wise."
As for ʿaṣībun (ʿaṣīb), Abu 'Ubayda said: ʿaṣīb is the severe one who grips people with evil. He recited:

The interpretation of "ūlia Zayd" is: his nature and disposition made him enamoured. "Urʿida al-rajul" means: his anger made him tremble. "Suhiya ʿAmr" means: his wealth or ignorance made him heedless. "Uhrii'a" means: his fear and terror made him rush. For this reason, these people formed these nouns in the manner of the object. ﴿And before this (wa-min qablu)﴾, that is, before their coming to Lut, ﴿they used to do evil deeds (al-sayyi'āt)﴾, meaning their reprehensible act.

The first: they were his daughters from his own loins. This is said by Ibn 'Abbas.
If it is asked: How did he use the plural when there were only two?
The answer: The plural may be used for two, as in His saying: ﴿and We were witnesses to their judgment﴾ [al-Anbiya': 78].
The second: he meant the women of his community (ummah), because every prophet is the father of his community. The meaning is that he offered them marriage, or ordered them to be content with their wives. This is the position of Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatada, and Ibn Jurayj.

The first: such marriage was permissible in his law, and it was permissible at the beginning of Islam until it was abrogated (nusikha). This is said by al-Hasan.
The second: he offered them on condition that they embrace Islam. This is said by al-Zajjaj, and what confirms it is that offering them to them was contingent upon the contract of marriage, so it was permissible for it to be contingent upon another condition.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿They are purer for you (hunna aṭhharu lakum)﴾. Muqatil said: They are more lawful than having intercourse with men.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿So fear God (fa-ttaqū Allāh)﴾. Concerning this there are two views:
The first: fear His punishment. The second: fear His disobedience.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿and do not disgrace me regarding my guests (wa-lā tukhzūnī fī ḍayfī)﴾. Abu 'Amr and Nafi' vocalized the ya' of "ḍayfī" (with a short vowel). Concerning the meaning of this disgrace there are three views:
The first: it is disgrace (al-fadīḥa). This is said by Ibn 'Abbas.
The second: it is shame (al-istihyā'), and the meaning is: do not do to my guests an act which obliges me to feel shame, because the host is obliged to feel shame for every act that reaches his guest. The Arabs say: "Qad khazia al-rajul yakhzā khizāyatan" when he felt shame. The poet said:
"Of the white (women), she does not feel shame when the wind clings / her wrap to her, or when the jewelry slips from her neck."
The third: it means ruin (al-halāk), because the disgrace that falls upon the host in this situation obliges him to ruin. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned both.
Ibn Qutayba said: Here "ḍayf" is in the sense of "aḍyāf" (guests), and the singular indicates the plural, as you say: "These are my messenger and my agent (hā'ulā’i rasūlī wa-wakīlī)."

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Is there not among you a man who is rightly guided (rashīd)?﴾ Concerning what is intended by rashīd there are two views:
The first: a believer. The second: one who enjoins the good and forbids the evil. Both are related from Ibn 'Abbas.
Ibn al-Anbari said: It is permissible that rashīd means murshid (one who guides), so the meaning is: "Is there not among you a guide who admonishes you and makes known to you the ugliness of what you do?" Then rashīd is an attribute of the doer, like ʿalīm (knowing) and shahīd (witnessing). The words of the Exalted: ﴿You know we have no claim on your daughters (mā lanā fī banātika min ḥaqq)﴾. Concerning this there are two views:
The first: we have no need for them. This is said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.
The second: they are not wives for us, so that we would have a right to them. This is said by Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Qutayba.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿If only I had power against you (law anna lī bikum quwwatan)﴾, that is, a group stronger than you by which I could prevail over you. It was said: By power he meant force (al-baṭsh). ﴿Or that I might take refuge in a strong pillar (aw āwī ilā rukn shadīd)﴾, that is, that I might join with a clan and a faction that would protect me. The answer to "law" is omitted, with the estimate: "I would have stood between you and disobedience." "He takes refuge in a pillar among the pillars, / in a numerous host and a noble glory."
al-Ṭays means "much." It is said: "Atānā laban ṭays wa-sharāb ṭays," meaning: much.

They differed as to what time Lut said this. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that Lut had closed his door while the angels were with him in the house, and he was disputing with them and imploring them behind the door, while they were trying to force the door and sought to climb over the wall. When the angels saw the distress he was suffering, they said: "O Lut, we are messengers of your Lord. Open the door and leave us and them." So he opened the door and they entered. Jibril asked his Lord for permission to punish them, and He permitted him. So he struck their faces with his wing and blinded them. They withdrew saying: "Escape, escape! In the house of Lut are the most sorcerous people on earth!" They began to say: "O Lut, stay as you are until morning," threatening him. Lut said to them: "When is the time of their destruction?" They said: "The morning." He said: "If only you would destroy them now!" They said: "Is not the morning near?" Abu Salih related from Ibn 'Abbas: When they threatened him, he said to himself: "These people will leave me tomorrow, and I will remain with these (guests), and they will destroy me." So he said: "If only I had power against you."
I say: This applies only if we say that it was before he knew that they were angels. Others said: He only said this when they broke down his door and rushed upon him. Still others said: He said this when he forbade them from his guests and they refused.
In sum, by "rukn" he did not mean the support of God and His help, since he was never without that. He meant only the clan and the family.
Abu Hurayra related from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "May God have mercy on Lut; he used to take refuge in a strong pillar. God did not send any prophet after him except among a people of great kinship (tharwa) from his own people."

The words of the Exalted: ﴿They will never reach you (lan yaṣilū ilayka)﴾. Muqatil said: There is an implied element; its estimate is: "They will never reach you with evil." That is because they said to Lut: "We see with you men who have bewitched our eyes, so you will know tomorrow what you and your family will face." Then Jibril said to him: ﴿We are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you﴾.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿So travel with your family (fa-asri bi-ahlika)﴾. 'Asim, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i recited "fa-asri" with the hamza in pronunciation, from asraytu (I travelled by night). Ibn Kathir and Nafi' recited "fa-sri bi-ahlika" without a hamza, from saraytu (I travelled by night). Both are two dialects (lughatān). Al-Zajjaj said: It is said "saraytu" and "asraytu" when you travel at night. The poet said:
"I travelled with them until their mounts tired, / and even the fine horses, though not led by reins."
Al-Nabigha said:
"The Pleiades (al-Jawza') from which a sweeping (sāriya) wind swept over him, / driving the north wind upon him, a frozen hail."
They also related it as "saratā" (she travelled). As for "ahlika" (your family), Muqatil said: They are his wife and his two daughters, and the names of his two daughters were Ruthā and Zu'arathā. Al-Suddi said: The name of the elder was Rayya, and the name of the younger was ʿArūba, and by "his family" is meant his two daughters. As for "qiṭ‘" (a part), it is in the sense of "qiṭ‘a" (a portion). It is said: "Maḍā qiṭ‘un min al-layl," meaning: a portion of the night. Ibn 'Abbas said: By this he means: the last part of the night. Ibn Qutayba said: "bi-qiṭ‘" means: with a remnant that remains from its end. Ibn al-Anbari said: The mention of qiṭ‘ in the sense of qiṭ‘a is specific to the night, and one does not say: "ʿindī qiṭ‘un min al-thawb," meaning "I have a piece of the garment."

The words of the Exalted: ﴿and let none of you look back (wa-lā yaltafit minkum aḥad)﴾. Concerning this there are two views:
The first: it means: let none of you lag behind. This is said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.
The second: it is the well-known turning around (al-iltifāt), said by Mujahid and Muqatil.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verse 77–81 (part 2 of 2):

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿except your wife﴾. Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with the accusative on the ta' (ʾimraʾataka, with a fatha). Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Ibn Jammaz, from Abu Ja'far, read it with the nominative on the ta' (imraʾatuka, with a damma).

Al-Zajjaj said: Whoever reads with the accusative, the meaning is: "So set out with your family, except your wife." Whoever reads with the nominative, he takes it as referring to ﴿And let none of you look back, except your wife﴾. They were ordered to abandon looking back only so that they would not see the magnitude of the punishment that would descend upon them.

Ibn al-Anbari said this. On the reading with the nominative, the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), meaning: "But as for your wife, she will look back, and so there will befall her what befell them." When the exception is disjunctive, her looking back is an act of disobedience to her Lord, because He had recommended abandoning looking back.

Qatadah said: It was mentioned to us that she was with Lut when he left the town. When she heard the thunderous roar of the punishment, she looked back and said, "Oh, my people!" So a stone struck her and killed her. This is His saying: ﴿Indeed, what befalls them will befall her. Indeed, their appointed time is the morning﴾ for the punishment, ﴿the morning﴾.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Is not the morning near?﴾ The commentators said: The angels said, "Indeed their appointed time is the morning," and he (Lut) said, "I want it to be sooner than that." So they said to him: ﴿Is not the morning near?﴾

(p-143) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So when Our command came﴾ has three interpretations:

First: it is God's command to the angels to punish them. Second: the "command" means the punishment. Third: it means God's decree to punish them.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We made its highest part its lowest﴾. The pronoun (*kināya*, the pronoun referring back to its antecedent) refers to the overturned towns (*al-mu'tafikāt*), which were the towns of the people of Lot. We have mentioned them in (Bara'a [al-Tawba]: 70), and here we point to the story of their destruction. Ibn 'Abbas said: Gabriel commanded Lot to leave, saying: "Depart, and take out your sheep and your cattle." He said: "How can I do that when the gates of the city have been shut?" So Gabriel spread his wing, lifted him, his two daughters, and his property, and there was nothing with them, and he brought them out of the city. Gabriel asked his Lord and said: "My Lord, entrust to me the destruction of these people." God revealed to him: "Undertake their destruction." When dawn broke, Gabriel came to them, lifted them on his wing, and rose with them until the birds in the air did not know where they were going. Then he overturned them upon them, and they heard a tremendous crash. Lot's wife turned around, and Gabriel struck her with a stone and killed her. Then he rose until he looked down upon the earth, and began to pursue them, their travelers, their herdsmen, and whoever had gone out of the town, and he stoned them until he had killed them. Al-Suddi said: Gabriel uprooted the earth from seven earths, carried it until he reached the lowest heaven, until the people of the heaven heard the barking of their dogs, and then he overturned it. Others said: They were five villages, the greatest of which was Sodom, and the people numbered four thousand thousand. It is also said: each village had one hundred thousand fighters. When he raised it up to the sky, no vessel broke for them and nothing fell, until he overturned it upon them. It is said: one of the five was saved, as it did not do the deeds of the others. Sa'id ibn Jubayr stood alone, saying: Gabriel and Michael were the ones who turned it over.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We rained upon it﴾: regarding the pronoun there are two views:

One: it refers back to the towns. Two: it refers back to the nation.

Regarding *al-sijjil* there are seven views:

First: in Persian it is *sang* and *gil*; *sing* means stone, and *gil* means clay. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Mujahid said: its first part is stone and its last part is clay. Al-Dahhak said: it means baked brick. Ibn Qutayba said: whoever holds this view takes as evidence His saying: ﴿stones of clay﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 33], meaning baked brick. Al-Farra' related that it is clay that has been baked until it became like millstones.

Second: it is a sea suspended in the air between the heaven and the earth, and from it the stones descended. This was said by 'Ikrima.

Third: *al-sijjil* is the name of the lowest heaven, so the meaning is: stones from the lowest heaven. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

Fourth: it is the hard, solid stone. This was said by Abu 'Ubayda, who recited for Ibn Muqbil:

"And a troop who strike the helmets from the side, a blow the champions have enjoined upon one another, *sijjīnā*."

(p-145) Ibn Qutayba rejected this view, saying: this is with a *nūn*, and that is with a *lām*; in this line it is *fi'īl* from *sajantu*, meaning I imprisoned, as if it fixes its companion in place.

Fifth: His saying "from *sijjīl*" is like your saying "from *sijill*", meaning: from what was written for them to be punished with. This is the choice of al-Zajjaj.

Sixth: it is from *asjaltuhu*, meaning I sent him, so it is as if they were sent upon them.

Seventh: it is from *asjalt*, meaning when you give. Al-Zajjaj related both of these views.

Regarding His saying: ﴿layered﴾ there are three views:

First: one part follows another. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Second: arranged in rows. This was said by 'Ikrima and Qatada. Third: one part was piled upon another, because it was clay that was gathered and made into stones. This was said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿marked﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, branded, taken from *al-sawma*, which is the mark.

Regarding its mark there are six views:

First: whiteness in redness. This was related by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Hasan said the same.

Second: they were sealed, so the stone was white with a black spot, or black with a white spot. This was related by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas.

Third: they were striped with black and red. This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

Fourth: upon them was a sprinkling of red with red lines in the shape of the veins of a date-cluster. This was said by 'Ikrima and Qatada.

Fifth: they were marked with a sign by which it was known that they were not stones of this world. This was said by Ibn Jurayj.

Sixth: upon each stone was the name of its owner. This was said by al-Rabi'. It is related from some who saw those stones that he said: they were like the heads of camels, like the resting places of camels, and like a man's fist.

Regarding His saying, the Exalted: ﴿with your Lord﴾ there are four views:

First: the meaning is: they came from your Lord. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil.

Second: "with your Lord" means prepared. This was said by Abu Bakr al-Huzali.

Third: the meaning is: this marking attached to these stones with God, as a notice of the execution of His power and the severity of His punishment. This was said by Ibn al-Anbari.

Fourth: the meaning of His saying "with your Lord" is: in His treasuries, from which nothing is disposed except by His permission.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And it is not far from the wrongdoers﴾. Regarding who is meant by "the wrongdoers" here, there are three views:

First: the wrongdoers here are the disbelievers of Quraysh, whom God warned with it. This was said by most scholars.

Second: it is general to every wrongdoer. Qatada said: By God, God has not spared any wrongdoer from it after the people of Lot, so fear God and be cautious of Him.

Third: they are the people of Lot, so the meaning is: "it is not far from the wrongdoers," that is, from the people of Lot. The meaning is: it would not miss them. This was said by al-Farra'.
