Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verse 84–85:

(p-147) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And to Madyan﴾ — we have already mentioned it in (al-A'raf: 85).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not diminish the measure and the balance﴾ — meaning: do not cheat (tutaffifu). They used to cheat in measure and weight despite their disbelief.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, I see you in prosperity﴾ — concerning this there are two opinions:

One of them: it means cheap prices. This was said by Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, and Mujahid.

The second: it means abundance of wealth. This is also related from Ibn Abbas, and Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said likewise. al-Farra' said: your wealth is abundant and your prices are cheap, so what need do you have for dishonest weighing and measuring?

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, I fear for you the punishment of an encompassing day﴾ — concerning this there are three opinions:

One of them: it means high prices. This was said by Ibn Abbas. Mujahid said: drought, barrenness, and high prices.

The second: the punishment in this world, which is what befell them. This was said by Muqatil.

The third: the punishment of the Fire in the Hereafter. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Give full measure and weight with justice﴾ — meaning: complete that with justice. Al-ifa' (إيفاء) means completion. ﴿And do not commit abuse on the earth, causing corruption﴾ — by diminishing the measure and the balance.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verse 84–85:

(p-147) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And to Madyan﴾ — we have already mentioned it in (al-A'raf: 85).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not diminish the measure and the balance﴾ — meaning: do not cheat (tutaffifu). They used to cheat in measure and weight despite their disbelief.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, I see you in prosperity﴾ — concerning this there are two opinions:

One of them: it means cheap prices. This was said by Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, and Mujahid.

The second: it means abundance of wealth. This is also related from Ibn Abbas, and Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said likewise. al-Farra' said: your wealth is abundant and your prices are cheap, so what need do you have for dishonest weighing and measuring?

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, I fear for you the punishment of an encompassing day﴾ — concerning this there are three opinions:

One of them: it means high prices. This was said by Ibn Abbas. Mujahid said: drought, barrenness, and high prices.

The second: the punishment in this world, which is what befell them. This was said by Muqatil.

The third: the punishment of the Fire in the Hereafter. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Give full measure and weight with justice﴾ — meaning: complete that with justice. Al-ifa' (إيفاء) means completion. ﴿And do not commit abuse on the earth, causing corruption﴾ — by diminishing the measure and the balance.

[p-148] His saying, the Exalted: ﴿What Allah leaves you (baqiyyat Allah) is better for you﴾. On this there are eight opinions:

The first: what Allah leaves you of lawful provision after giving full measure and weight is better than defrauding people. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

[p-149] The second: the provision of Allah is better for you. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, and Sufyan held this view.

The third: obedience to Allah is better for you. This was said by Mujahid and al-Zajjaj.

The fourth: your share from Allah is better for you. This was said by Qatada.

The fifth: the mercy of Allah is better for you. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The sixth: the command of Allah is better for you. This was said by al-Rabi'.

The seventh: the reward of Allah in the Hereafter is better for you. This was said by Muqatil.

The eighth: the watchfulness of Allah is better for you. This was mentioned by al-Farra'.

Al-Hasan al-Basri recited it as "taqiyyat Allah" (with a ta' instead of the ba') [the recitation (qira'a) variant].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿if you are believers﴾. He made faith the condition for it being good for them, because if they believed in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, they would recognise the truth of what he says.

On His saying: ﴿and I am not a guardian over you﴾ there are three opinions:

The first: I was not commanded to fight you or to compel you to faith.

The second: I was not commanded to watch over you when you measure, lest you defraud.

The third: I cannot protect you from the punishment of Allah if it befalls you.

His saying, the Exalted: "Does your prayer (aṣalawātuka) command you..." Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf and Hafs recited "aṣalātuka" (in the singular), which is the form of unity.

Regarding what is meant by his prayers (ṣalawāt) there are three opinions: the first, that it is his religion; this was said by 'Ata'. The second, that it is his recitation; this was said by al-A'mash. The third, that it refers to the well-known prescribed prayers. Shu'ayb was one who prayed much.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿or that we should do with our wealth what we please﴾. Al-Farra' said: the meaning of the verse is: "Does your prayer command you that we abandon what our fathers worshipped, or that we abandon doing with our wealth what we please?"

[p-150] On the meaning of the sentence according to the reading of those who recited with the nun (naf'alu), there are two views:

The first: their action regarding their wealth was defrauding and cheating, and this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The meaning, then, is: "We have agreed among ourselves upon that."

The second: they used to clip the dirhams and dinars, and he forbade them from this; this was said by Ibn Zayd. Al-Qurazi said: they were punished for clipping the dirhams. Ibn al-Anbari said: al-Dahhak ibn Qays al-Fihri recited "mā tasha'" (with ta'), and he linked "an taf'ala" to "an tatruka" and dispensed with the implied pronoun. Sufyan al-Thawri said: the meaning of this recitation is that he commanded them to pay zakat and they refused. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, al-Dahhak and Ibn Abi 'Abla recited "aw an taf'ala fī amwālinā mā tashā'" with ta' in both places; the meaning of this recitation is like the meaning of al-Fihri's recitation.

On His saying: ﴿Indeed you are the forbearing, the rightly guided﴾ there are four opinions:

The first: they said it mockingly to him. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and Qatada and al-Farra' held this view.

The second: they said to him: "Indeed you are the foolish, the ignorant," and he expressed it by this, as mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

The third: they reviled him, saying that he was neither forbearing nor rightly guided, so Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, praised him and said: "Rather, you are indeed the forbearing, the rightly guided, not as the disbelievers said of you." This was related by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi from Abu al-Hasan al-Musaysi.

The fourth: they actually acknowledged to him forbearance and rectitude, and said: "You are forbearing and rightly guided, so why do you forbid us from doing with our wealth what we please?" This was related by al-Mawardi, and Ibn Kaysan went in this direction.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿If I am upon clear evidence from my Lord﴾. Its explanation has already been given [Hud 28 and 63].

[p-151] On His saying: ﴿and He has given me from Himself good provision﴾ there are three opinions:

The first: that it is what is lawful. Ibn 'Abbas said: Shu'ayb was a man of much wealth.

The second: prophethood. The third: knowledge and understanding.

Al-Zajjaj said: the answer to the condition here is omitted, and the meaning is: "If I am upon clear evidence from my Lord, shall I follow error?" He omitted the answer because the addressees know the meaning, and a similar case has already passed.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and I do not intend to oppose you in what I forbid you from﴾. Qatada said: I would not forbid you from a matter and then commit it myself. Al-Zajjaj said: I do not intend, by opposing you, to aim at committing it.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿I intend only reform as far as I am able﴾. That is: what I command you with is only the reform of your affairs to the extent of my ability. The extent of my ability is conveying to you, not compelling you.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And my success is only by Allah﴾. The people of Medina and Ibn 'Amir read the ta' of "tawfiqī" with a fatha. The meaning of the sentence is: my attaining the truth in seeking your reform is only by Allah. ﴿Upon Him I have relied﴾: that is, I have entrusted my affair to Him. This is because they had threatened him with their words: ﴿We will surely expel you, O Shu'ayb﴾ [al-A'raf 88]. ﴿And to Him I turn back﴾: that is, I return.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Let not my opposition bring upon you (yajrimannakum shiqāqī)﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Nafi' gave this ya' a vowel. Al-Zajjaj said: let not your enmity toward me cause you to be punished.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the people of Lot are not far from you﴾. On this there are two views:

The first: they were near to their dwellings.

The second: that it is a reference to what Shu'ayb brought. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: obedience to Allah is better for you. This was said by Mujahid and al-Zajjaj.

The fourth: your share from Allah is better for you. This was said by Qatada.

The fifth: the mercy of Allah is better for you. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The sixth: the command of Allah is better for you. This was said by al-Rabi'.

The seventh: the reward of Allah in the Hereafter is better for you. This was said by Muqatil.

The eighth: the watchfulness of Allah is better for you. This was mentioned by al-Farra'.

The first: I was not commanded to fight you or to compel you to faith.

The second: I was not commanded to watch over you when you measure, lest you defraud.

The third: I cannot protect you from the punishment of Allah if it befalls you.

The second: they said to him: "Indeed you are the foolish, the ignorant," and he expressed it by this, as mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

The third: they reviled him, saying that he was neither forbearing nor rightly guided, so Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, praised him and said: "Rather, you are indeed the forbearing, the rightly guided, not as the disbelievers said of you." On His saying: ﴿Indeed you are the forbearing, the rightly guided﴾ there are four opinions:

The first: they said it mockingly to him. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and Qatada and al-Farra' held this view.

The second: they said to him: "Indeed you are the foolish, the ignorant," and he expressed it by this, as mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

The third: they reviled him, saying that he was neither forbearing nor rightly guided, so Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, praised him and said: "Rather, you are indeed the forbearing, the rightly guided, not as the disbelievers said of you." This was related by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi from Abu al-Hasan al-Musaysi.

The fourth: they actually acknowledged to him forbearance and rectitude, and said: "You are forbearing and rightly guided, so why do you forbid us from doing with our wealth what we please?" This was related by al-Mawardi, and Ibn Kaysan went in this direction.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿If I am upon clear evidence from my Lord﴾. Its explanation has already been given [Hud 28 and 63].

[p-151] On His saying: ﴿and He has given me from Himself good provision﴾ there are three opinions:

The first: that it is what is lawful. Ibn 'Abbas said: Shu'ayb was a man of much wealth.

The second: prophethood. The third: knowledge and understanding.

Al-Zajjaj said: the answer to the condition here is omitted, and the meaning is: "If I am upon clear evidence from my Lord, shall I follow error?" He omitted the answer because the addressees know the meaning, and a similar case has already passed.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and I do not intend to oppose you in what I forbid you from﴾. Qatada said: I would not forbid you from a matter and then commit it myself. Al-Zajjaj said: I do not intend, by opposing you, to aim at committing it.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿I intend only reform as far as I am able﴾. That is: what I command you with is only the reform of your affairs to the extent of my ability. The extent of my ability is conveying to you, not compelling you.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And my success is only by Allah﴾. The people of Medina and Ibn 'Amir read the ta' of "tawfiqī" with a fatha. The meaning of the sentence is: my attaining the truth in seeking your reform is only by Allah. ﴿Upon Him I have relied﴾: that is, I have entrusted my affair to Him. This is because they had threatened him with their words: ﴿We will surely expel you, O Shu'ayb﴾ [al-A'raf 88]. ﴿And to Him I turn back﴾: that is, I return.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Let not my opposition bring upon you (yajrimannakum shiqāqī)﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Nafi' gave this ya' a vowel. Al-Zajjaj said: let not your enmity toward me cause you to be punished.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the people of Lot are not far from you﴾. On this there are two views:

The first: they were near to their dwellings.

The second: they were recent in regard to the punishment of the people of Lot. Al-Zajjaj said: the destruction of the people of Lot was the nearest of the destructions that they knew of. Ibn al-Anbari said: he used the singular "ba'īd" because he removed it from describing the people and made it an adjective for an omitted place, its implied meaning being: "And the people of Lot are not from you in a far place."

[p-152] His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed my Lord is Merciful and Loving﴾. The meaning of "Merciful" has already been given.

As for "Loving" (wadūd): Ibn al-Anbari said its meaning is: the one who loves His servants, from their saying: "waddadtu al-rajul, awaddu-hu, wuddan, wadan, widdan," and it is said: "waddadtu al-rajul widādan, widādatan, wadādatan." Al-Khattabi said: it is a name derived from "wudd," and in it there are two aspects:

The first: that it is fa'ūl in the sense of maf'ūl, as it is said: "rajul hayūb" meaning mahīb (one who is feared), and "furs rakūb" meaning markūb (one who is ridden). So Allah, glorified is He, is loved (mawdūd) in the hearts of His friends because of His kindness to them, which they recognise.

The other aspect: that it means the one who loves (wādd), that is, He loves His righteous servants, meaning that He is pleased with them by accepting their deeds. Its meaning may also be that He makes them beloved to His creation, as in His saying: ﴿The Most Merciful will appoint for them affection (wudd)﴾ [Maryam 96].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We do not understand much of what you say﴾. Ibn al-Anbari said: its meaning is: we do not understand the correctness of much of what you say, because they practised a religion other than it. It is possible also that, because they found it burdensome, they were as if they did not understand it.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And indeed we see you among us as weak﴾. On this there are four opinions:

The first: blind. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and Qatada said: he was blind. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said that the tribe of Himyar calls the blind man "weak."

The second: humble, lowly. This was said by al-Hasan, Abu Ruq and Muqatil.

Abu Ruq claimed that Allah never sent a blind prophet, nor a prophet with any disability.

The third: weak of sight. This was said by Sufyan.

The fourth: unable to act in earning livelihood. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

[p-153] His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And were it not for your clan, we would have stoned you﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: were it not for your kin, we would have killed you by stoning, and stoning is one of the worst kinds of killing. His clan were of their religion, and so for that reason they showed inclination toward them and honoured them. Some of them mentioned that stoning here means insult and harm.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And you are not mighty against us﴾. On this there are two views: the first, not noble; the second, not able to prevent us from killing you.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Is my clan more esteemed by you than Allah?﴾ The people of Kufa and Ya'qub made the ya' of "rahṭī" quiescent. The meaning: "Do you regard my clan on my account, and not regard Allah on my account?"

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and you have put Him behind your backs﴾. On the pronoun (hā' al-kināya) there are two opinions:

The first: that it refers to Allah, the Exalted. This was said by the majority. Al-Farra' said: the meaning is: you have thrown away the command of Allah behind your backs. Al-Zajjaj said: the Arabs say of everyone who pays no attention to a matter: "So-and-so has put this matter behind his back." The poet said:

"Tamim ibn Qays, do not let my need be behind the back, so that its answer does not become difficult for me."

The second: that it is a reference to what Shu'ayb brought. This was said by Mujahid.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed my Lord is encompassing of what you do﴾: that is, He is knowing of your deeds, and so He will recompense you for them. What follows this has already been explained up to His saying: ﴿You will know﴾ [al-An'am 135].

If someone asks: why did he say here "sawfa" and in another surah "fasawfa" [al-An'am 135]?

The answer: both are good in the usage of the Arabs. If they include the fa', it indicates the connection of what follows to what precedes; if they drop it, they make the first speech complete, and what follows is a new beginning, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed Allah commands you to slaughter a cow. They said: Do you take us in ridicule?﴾ [al-Baqara 67]. The meaning is: "They said: Do you take us..." with the fa', but the fa' was omitted because what came before was complete. Imru' al-Qays said:

"She said: By Allah's oath, you have no means, and I do not see your error being cleared away.
I went out with her walking, dragging behind us upon our traces the hems of a striped, fringed cloak."

Ibn al-Anbari said: he meant: "So she went out," and he dropped the fa' because what preceded was complete. It is also narrated: "So I went out with her walking."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And watch, I am with you a watcher﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: watch for the punishment, for I am watching for the reward.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the cry seized those who had wronged﴾. The commentators said: Jibril cried out at them and they died in their places. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: Allah punished the people of Madyan with three kinds of punishment. A quaking seized them in their homes until they feared it would fall upon them, so they went out of them, and a severe heat befell them, so Allah sent a cloud-shade, and they called to one another: "Come to the shade!" They all entered the shade, and then a single cry was let out upon them, and they all died. Ibn 'Abbas said: no two nations were ever punished with one punishment except the people of Shu'ayb and Salih. As for the people of Salih, the cry seized them from beneath them; as for the people of Shu'ayb, it seized them from above them. A cloud appeared to them like a canopy, in which there was wind, after the wind had been withheld from them; they came to it seeking shade beneath it, and it burned them.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿As Thamud perished (ba'idat)﴾: that is, as Thamud was destroyed.

[p-155] Ibn Qutayba said: it is said "ba'ida yab'adu" when his distance is destruction, and "ba'uda yab'udu" when he goes far away.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verses 96–97:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly sent Musa with Our signs﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: with Our signs (ʿalamat), which indicate the truth of his prophethood. ﴿And a clear authority﴾, i.e., a manifest proof.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But they followed the command of Pharaoh﴾, which is what he commanded them of worshipping him and taking him as a god. ﴿And the command of Pharaoh was not right-guiding﴾, i.e., it did not guide to any good.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verses 96–97:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly sent Musa with Our signs﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: with Our signs (ʿalamat), which indicate the truth of his prophethood. ﴿And a clear authority﴾, i.e., a manifest proof.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But they followed the command of Pharaoh﴾, which is what he commanded them of worshipping him and taking him as a god. ﴿And the command of Pharaoh was not right-guiding﴾, i.e., it did not guide to any good.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verse 98:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He will lead his people on the Day of Resurrection﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: It is said, "I preceded the people (qadamtu al-qawm) and I precede them (aqdumuhum), qadman and qudumen," when you go ahead of them. The meaning is that he leads them to the Fire. This is supported by His saying: ﴿and bring them down into the Fire﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "awradahum" means "adkhalahum," he caused them to enter. Qatada said: He walks ahead of them until he rushes them upon the Fire.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿What an evil watering-place to be brought to!﴾ The exegetes said: al-wird is the place that one comes to (for water). Ibn al-Anbari said: al-wird is a verbal noun (masdar) whose meaning is al-wurud (the coming). The Arabs use it to mean the place that is come to (al-mawrud). So the paraphrase of the phrase is: "And what an evil place of entry is the place entered, the Fire."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verse 99:

The Almighty's saying: ﴿And they were followed in this world by a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection [too]﴾.

Regarding "in this [world]" there are two opinions:

(p-156) The first: that in this world it is drowning, and in the Hereafter it is the punishment of the Fire. This is the view of al-Kalbi and Muqatil.

The second: that it is the curse in this world from the believers, and in the Hereafter from the angels. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿Wretched is the gift that is given﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: al-rifd (the gift, reward) is a bounty; he says: "The curse is a wretched bounty." It is said: "rafadtuhu arfiduhu" when you give him and help him. And al-marfud is the one who is given.

That is one of the accounts of the towns (ʾanbāʾ al-qurā) — (ﷺ) no; let me render it precisely.

"That is among the news of the towns." He means what has preceded of the report concerning the destroyed towns. "We relate it to you." That is, We inform you of it. "Of them, some are standing and some are reaped." Qatadah said: "The standing is that whose place can still be seen, and the reaped is that whose trace cannot be seen." Ibn Qutaybah said: "The standing is that which is visible to the eye, and the reaped is that which has been annihilated and mown down." Al-Zajjaj said: "The standing is that whose walls remain, and the reaped is that which was swallowed up by the earth and whose trace has been effaced."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verse 101:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not wrong them﴾, meaning: by the punishment and destruction. ﴿But they wronged themselves﴾ by disbelief and acts of disobedience. ﴿So their gods did not avail them at all﴾, meaning: they did not benefit them nor did they ward off anything from them ﴿when the command of your Lord came﴾ with destruction. ﴿And they added nothing to them but perdition﴾, meaning the gods. Regarding "tatbib" (perdition, ruin) there are three views:

The first: that it means ruin (at-takhsir, loss). This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas, and Mujahid and Qatadah said the same. Ibn Qutaybah and al-Zajjaj preferred this view. The second: that it means evil, as said by Ibn Zayd. The third: that it means destruction and annihilation, as said by Abu Ubaydah.

If it is asked: the gods are inanimate, so how does He say ﴿they added to them﴾? There are two answers to this:

One: that is, the worship of them did not add anything except [ruin].

The second: that on the Day of Resurrection they will become a source of help against them, and so they will increase them in evil.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verse 102:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And such is the seizing of your Lord﴾, meaning: just as was mentioned of the destruction of the nations and their being seized with punishment, such is the seizing of your Lord. ﴿When He seizes the towns while they are wrongdoers﴾. He described the towns with wrongdoing, while what is meant is their people. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The wrongdoing (zulm) here means disbelief (kufr)."

Allah says: ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign﴾, meaning what was mentioned of the punishment of the nations and their seizure. The word āyah (sign) means a lesson and an admonition. ﴿That is a Day on which mankind will be gathered﴾, because creation will be assembled on it, and both the righteous and the wicked will witness it, as will the people of the heavens and the earth. ﴿And We do not delay it﴾. Zayd narrated from Yaʿqub, and Abu Zayd from al-Mufaddal, reading "wa-mā yuʾakhkhiruhu" with the letter yāʾ (in the third person). The meaning is: We do not delay that Day except until a known term, which none knows but Allah.

Allah says: ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign﴾, meaning what was mentioned of the punishment of the nations and their seizure. The word āyah (sign) means a lesson and an admonition. ﴿That is a Day on which mankind will be gathered﴾, because creation will be assembled on it, and both the righteous and the wicked will witness it, as will the people of the heavens and the earth. ﴿And We do not delay it﴾. Zayd narrated from Yaʿqub, and Abu Zayd from al-Mufaddal, reading "wa-mā yuʾakhkhiruhu" with the letter yāʾ (in the third person). The meaning is: We do not delay that Day except until a known term, which none knows but Allah.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zād al-Masīr) on Sūrah Hūd, verses 105–108**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿On the day it comes﴾. Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr and al-Kisāʾī read *yawma yaʾti* with a *yāʾ* (*yāʾ*) when connected, and they omitted it when pausing. However, Ibn Kathīr would pause with the *yāʾ* and connect with the *yāʾ*. ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir and Ḥamzah read it without a *yāʾ*, both when connected and when pausing.

Al-Zajjāj said: What the grammarians prefer is *yawma yaʾtī* with the *yāʾ* retained. What is in the *muṣḥaf* (the written copy of the Qur'an), and what most of the recitations follow, is the kasra on the *tāʾ*. The tribe of Hudhayl often uses the omission of these *yāʾs*. Al-Khalīl and Sībawayh have also reported that the Arabs say *lā adri* (I do not know), omitting the *yāʾ* and making do with the kasra, and they claim that this is due to frequent usage. Al-Farrāʾ said: Every quiescent *yāʾ* preceded by a kasra, or every quiescent *wāw* preceded by a damma, the Arabs omit, and they make do with the kasra for the *yāʾ* and with the damma for the *wāw*. One of them recited to me:

*Your palm is a palm that does not give a dirham in generosity, while the other gives blood with the sword.*

The exegetes said: His saying, *yawma yaʾtī*, means: that day comes. No soul speaks except by the permission of Allah. So all creatures are silent, except those whom Allah permits to speak. It was also said that what is meant by this speech is intercession (*shafāʿah*, the request made on another's behalf for forgiveness or mercy).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Among them is the wretched﴾. Ibn ʿAbbās said: Among them are those for whom wretchedness has been decreed, and among them are those for whom happiness has been decreed.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿For them therein is groaning and wailing﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions:

The first: *zafīr* is like the braying of a donkey in the chest, which is the beginning of its bray, and *shahīq* is like the braying of a donkey in the throat, which is the last of its braying. This was narrated by Abū Ṣāliḥ from Ibn ʿAbbās, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Muqātil and al-Farrāʾ also said it. Al-Zajjāj said: *al-zafīr* is the intense and ugly moaning, and *al-shahīq* is the intense moaning that rises very high, and both are sounds of those in distress. The grammarians of Kufa and Basra claimed that *al-zafīr* is like the beginning of the donkey's voice in braying, and *al-shahīq* is like the end of its voice in braying.

The second: *al-zafīr* is in the throat, and *al-shahīq* is in the chest. This was narrated by al-Ḍaḥḥāk from Ibn ʿAbbās, and Abū al-ʿĀliyah and al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas also said it. In another narration from Ibn ʿAbbās: *al-zafīr* is the strong sound, and *al-shahīq* is the weak sound. Ibn Fāris said: *al-shahīq* is the opposite of *al-zafīr*, because *al-shahīq* is the drawing back of breath and *al-zafīr* is the expelling of breath. Others said: *al-zafīr* means the intense, derived from *al-zafr*, which is carrying a load on the back because of its heaviness; and *al-shahīq* is the long, extended breath, derived from their saying: a lofty mountain (*jabal shāhiq*), meaning tall.

The third: *al-zafīr* is the braying of the donkey and *al-shahīq* is the braying of mules. This was said by Ibn al-Sāʾib.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾. Regarding this, there are two well-known opinions:

The first: they are the heavens known to us and the earth known to us. Ibn Qutaybah and Ibn al-Anbārī said: The Arabs have several expressions for eternity. They say: I will not do that as long as the night and day alternate, as long as the heavens and earth endure, as long as the *jirrah* and *dirrah* alternate, as long as camels make their soft sound, and other similar expressions in great number. They assumed that these things do not change, so Allah addressed them in what they use in their speech.

The second: they are the heavens and earth of Paradise and Hell.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Except what your Lord wills﴾. Concerning the exception mentioned with regard to the people of the Fire, there are seven opinions:

The first: the exception concerns the monotheists (*muwaḥḥidūn*) who will leave (the Fire) through intercession. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

The second: it is an exception that will not be carried out. You say: By Allah, I will strike you, except if I see otherwise, while your resolve is to strike him. This was mentioned by al-Farrāʾ, and it is the meaning of the saying of Abū Ṣāliḥ from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning *illā mā shāʾa rabbuk*: He said: He has willed that they remain therein forever. Al-Zajjāj said: The benefit of this is that if He had willed to show them mercy, He would have shown it to them, but He informed us that they will remain forever.

The third: the meaning is: abiding therein forever, except that Allah, may He be exalted, commands the Fire so that it consumes them and annihilates them, then He renews their creation, and so the exception refers to that state. This was said by Ibn Masʿūd.

The fourth: *illā* is in the sense of *siwā* (other than). You say: If there were with us a man other than Zayd (*law kāna maʿanā rajul illā Zayd*), meaning other than Zayd. So the meaning is: abiding therein for the duration of the heavens and the earth, other than what your Lord wills of eternity and increase. This is the choice of al-Farrāʾ. Ibn Qutaybah said: A similar usage in speech is that you say: I will house you in this house for a year, except what I wish, meaning: other than what I wish to add to you.

The fifth: when they are gathered and resurrected, they are under the conditions of the Resurrection. So the exception applies to their eternity in the measure of their standing for reckoning. The meaning is: abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except for the length of their standing for the reckoning. This was mentioned by al-Zajjāj. Ibn Kaysān said: The exception refers to their stay in this world, in the intermediate state (*barzakh*), and in standing for reckoning. Ibn Qutaybah said: So the meaning is: abiding in the Fire and abiding in the Garden for the duration of the heaven and earth, except what your Lord wills of their remaining in this world before that. It is as though he made the duration of the heaven and earth to mean eternity, according to how the Arabs used it, even though both may change. He made the exception of will from their duration, because the people of the Garden and the Fire had been at a time during the duration of the heaven and earth in this world, not in the Garden or the Fire.

The sixth: the exception applies to the fact that they will have therein groaning and wailing, except what your Lord wills of the kinds of punishment that were not mentioned. Likewise, the people of the Garden have bliss of what was mentioned, and for them there is what your Lord wills of what was not mentioned. This was also mentioned by al-Zajjāj.

The seventh: *illā* is in the sense of *kamā* (as). From it is His saying: ﴿And do not marry what your fathers married of women, except what has already passed﴾ [al-Nisāʾ 4:22]. This was mentioned by al-Thaʿlabī.

As for the exception concerning the people of the Garden, there are six opinions:

The first: it is an exception that will not be carried out. The second: *illā* is in the sense of *siwā*. The third: it refers to their standing for reckoning and their staying in the graves. The fourth: it means: except what He wills to increase for them of the bliss that was not mentioned. The fifth: *illā* is in the sense of *kamā*, and these opinions have already been explained. The sixth: the exception refers to the staying of those among the monotheists who remained in the Fire, after which they were admitted to the Garden. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Muqātil. Ibn Qutaybah said: Then the exception from eternity will be the stay of the sinners among the Muslims in the Fire. It is as though he said: except what your Lord wills of bringing the sinners out to the Garden, and abiding in the Garden except what your Lord wills of admitting the sinners to the Fire for a period.

The reciters differed over *suʿidū* (they were made happy). Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, and Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim read *saʿidū* with a fatḥah on the *sīn*. Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī and Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim read it with a ḍammah on it. Both are dialectal forms.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿A gift unbroken﴾. *ʿAṭāʾan* is in the accusative by what the sentence implies, as though he said: He gave them bliss as a gift. *Al-majdhūdh* means the cut off. Ibn Qutaybah said: It is said *jadhadtu* and *jadadtu*, and *jadhafta* and *jadafta*, meaning: when you cut.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verse 110:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We had certainly given Moses the Book﴾, meaning the Torah, "but it was disputed about." Some believed in it and some denied it, just as your people did with the Qur'an. The exegetes (mufassirun) said: this is a consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if not for a word that preceded from your Lord﴾. Ibn Abbas said: he means, "I have delayed your nation until the Day of Resurrection, and were it not for that, I would have hastened the punishment of those who denied you." Ibn Qutaybah said: "Were it not for a respite granted to them until the Day of Judgment, it would have been decided between them in this world." Ibn Jarir said: (p-163) "[the word] that preceded from your Lord, that He does not hasten the punishment upon His creation, it would have been decided between those of them who affirmed and those who denied, by destroying the deniers and saving the affirmers."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed they are in disquieting doubt about it﴾, that is, about the Qur'an. "Disquieting" (murib) means causing suspicion (raib).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verse 111:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, all﴾ refers to all of those whose stories are related in this surah. Muqatil said: it means the disbelievers of this community. It was also said: the meaning is: "And indeed, all of them are creation or humans, [and] He will surely repay them in full" (*la-yuwaffiyannahum*). Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i recited *wa-inna* with a doubled *nun* and *lamma* with a light (single) *mim*. The *lam* in *lamma* is the *lam* of emphasis (*lam al-tawkid*), which entered upon *ma*, and it is the predicate of *inna*. The *lam* in *la-yuwaffiyannahum* is the *lam* that introduces an oath (*lam al-qasam*), and the implied meaning is: "By God, He will surely repay them in full," and *ma* entered to separate the two *lams*. Makki ibn Abi Talib said: it was also said that *ma* is superfluous, but it entered to separate the two *lams* which introduce the oath, and both of them are fatha-vowelled, so *ma* separated them. Ibn Kathir recited *wa-in* with a light *nun*, and likewise *lamma*. Sibawayh said: "One whom we trust told us that he heard some of the Arabs say: *in 'amran lamuntaliqun* (Indeed, 'Amr is surely departing), so they lighten *in* and make it operate (in the accusative)," and he recited:

*wa-wajhin hasani al-nahri ka-anna thadyayhi huqqan*
(And a face beautiful of throat, as if its two breasts were two ivory cases)

Nafi' and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, recited *wa-in* with a light *nun*, and *lamma* with a doubled *mim*. The meaning is: "There is no one, all of them, except [that He will repay them]." This is like your saying: "I asked you *lamma* you did [it]," meaning "except that you did [it]." A similar usage is His saying: ﴿In every soul there is surely a guardian over it﴾ [al-Tariq: 4]. Hamzah, Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs from 'Asim recited *wa-inna* with a doubled *nun*, and *lamma* also with a doubled *mim*. Abu 'Ali said: this reading is problematic, because just as it is not good to say *inna Zaydan illa muntaliqun*, likewise it is not good to double *inna* and to double *lamma*. He reported from al-Kisa'i that he said: "I do not know the grammatical basis for doubling *lamma*," and he did not go far in what he said. Makki ibn Abi Talib said: the original form of it is *laman ma*, then the *nun* was assimilated into the *mim*, so three *mims* came together in pronunciation, and the *mim* that is kasra-vowelled was deleted. The implied sense is: "And indeed, all of them, from among creation, He will surely repay them in full." He said: it was also said that the implied form is *laman ma* with a fatha on the *mim* of *man*, so *ma* is superfluous, and one of the *mims* is deleted because of the repetition of the *mim* in pronunciation; the implied sense is: "creation, He will surely repay them in full," and the meaning of the statement is: "He will surely repay them the recompense of their deeds."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verse 112:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So remain upright as you have been commanded﴾. Ibn ʿUyaynah said: "Remain upright in the Qur'an." Ibn Qutaybah said: "Proceed in what you have been commanded."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and those who turn back with you﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Those who turn back with you from polytheism."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and do not transgress﴾. Concerning it there are three opinions:

One: "Do not transgress regarding the Qur'an, by making lawful and making unlawful what I have not commanded you." This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: "Do not disobey your Lord and do not oppose Him." This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The third: "Do not mix tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness) with doubt." This was said by Muqatil.

(p-165) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do not incline toward those who have done wrong﴾. 'Abd al-Warith related from Abu 'Amr that *tarkanu* (تَرْكَنُوا) was read with a fatha on the *ta'* and a damma on the *kaf*, and this is the qira'ah (recitation) of Qatadah. Harun related from Abu 'Amr that *tarkanu* (تَرْكَنُوا) was read with a fatha on the *ta'* and a kasra on the *kaf*. Mahbub related from Abu 'Amr that *tarkanu* (تَرْكَنُوا) was read with a kasra on the *ta'* and a fatha on the *kaf*. Ibn Abi 'Ablah read *tarkanu* (تَرْكَنُوا) with a damma on the *ta'* and a fatha on the *kaf*, in the passive form (*ma lam yusamma fa'iluh*).

Regarding the meaning of this *rukun* (inclining), there are four opinions.

The first: Do not lean toward the polytheists. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: Do not approve of their deeds. This was said by Abu al-'Aliyah. The third: Do not join the polytheists. This was said by Qatadah. The fourth: Do not flatter the wrongdoers. This was said by al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd.

As for His saying: ﴿lest the Fire touch you﴾, there are two interpretations. The first: lest the Fire afflict you. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: their wrongdoing will spread to you, just as fire spreads to burn what is near it. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you have no protectors besides Allah﴾. That is: you have no helpers who can protect you from the punishment.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verse 114:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And establish prayer at the two ends of the day﴾. As for the occasion of its revelation, ʿAlqamah and al-Aswad narrated from Ibn Masʿud that "a man said to the Prophet ﷺ: 'I took a woman in an orchard and kissed her, embraced her, lay close to her, and did everything with her except that I did not have intercourse with her.' (p-166) The Prophet ﷺ remained silent, and Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And establish prayer at the two ends of the day...﴾ — the verse. So he summoned the man and recited it to him. ʿUmar said: 'Is it for him alone, or for all people?' He said: 'No, rather it is for all people.'" In another narration from Ibn Masʿud: "A man had kissed a woman, so he came to the Messenger of Allah and mentioned that to him, and this verse was revealed. The man said: 'Is this verse for me?' He said: 'For whoever among my community acts upon it.'" Muʿadh ibn Jabal said: "I was sitting with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when a man came and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what do you say about a man who did with a woman what is not lawful for him, and he left nothing that a man may do with his wife except that he did it with her, except that he did not have intercourse with her?' The Prophet ﷺ said to him: 'Perform ablution well, then stand and pray.' So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse." Muʿadh said: "Is it for him alone, or for the Muslims in general?" He said: "Rather it is for the Muslims in general."

They differed concerning the name of this man. Abu Salih narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he was ʿAmr ibn Ghaziyyah al-Ansari, and this verse was revealed concerning him. He used to sell dates, and a woman came to him to buy dates from him; he was impressed by her, so he said: "In the house there are dates better than these; come with me until I give you some of them." Then he related something similar to the hadith of Muʿadh. Muqatil said: he was Abu Muqbil ʿAmir ibn Qays al-Ansari. Al-Hafiz al-Khatib Ahmad ibn ʿAli ibn Thabit mentioned that he was Abu al-Yusr Kaʿb ibn ʿAmr al-Ansari.

Regarding the one who said to the Prophet ﷺ, "Is it for him alone?", there are three opinions:

The first: he was Abu al-Yusr, the protagonist of the account. The second: Muʿadh ibn Jabal. The third: ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab.

As for the interpretation: His saying "And establish prayer" means: complete its bowing and its prostration.

As for "the two ends of the day," regarding the first end there are two views:

One: it is the Fajr prayer; this is the view of the majority. The second: it is the Zuhr prayer; related by Ibn Jarir.

Regarding the second end there are three views:

One: it is the Maghrib prayer; said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Zayd. The second: the ʿAsr prayer; said by Qatadah. And from al-Hasan, both views as above. The third: the Zuhr and ʿAsr prayers; said by Mujahid and al-Qurazi. And from al-Dahhak, the three views as above.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And at the approaches of the night﴾. Abu Jaʿfar and Shaybah read "wa-zulufan" with a damma on the lam. Abu ʿUbaydah said: "Zulaf" are the hours; its singular is "zulfah," meaning an hour, a station, and a nearness; from it Muzdalifah is named. Al-ʿAjjaj said: (p-168)

Swift one, whom weariness has folded, of what he traveled,
Folding the nights, hour by hour, then hour by hour,
Until the moon's crescent curved.

Ibn Qutaybah said: From it one says: "Azlafani kadha ʿindaka," meaning: he brought me near. And "al-mazalif" are the stations and steps; likewise "zulaf."

Regarding it, the commentators have two views:

One: it is the ʿAtamah prayer; narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿAwf from al-Hasan, and Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid; and Ibn Zayd said likewise.

The second: it is the Maghrib and ʿIsha prayers; also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas; Yunus narrated it from al-Hasan, and Mansur from Mujahid; and Qatadah, Muqatil, and al-Zajjaj said likewise.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, good deeds remove evil deeds﴾. Regarding what is meant by "good deeds," there are two views:

One: they are the five daily prayers; said by Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn al-Musayyab, Masruq, Mujahid, al-Qurazi, al-Dahhak, and the two Muqatils: Ibn Sulayman and Ibn Hayyan.

The second: they are "Subhan Allah," "al-Hamdu li-Llah," "La ilaha illa Allah," and "Allahu Akbar"; narrated by Mansur from Mujahid. The first is more sound, because the majority hold it, and there is a connected hadith from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, narrated by ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan: "That the Messenger of Allah ﷺ performed ablution and said: 'Whoever performs ablution like this ablution of mine, then prays Zuhr, will be forgiven what is between it and the Fajr prayer. (p-169) And whoever prays ʿAsr will be forgiven what is between it and the Zuhr prayer. And whoever prays Maghrib will be forgiven what is between it and the ʿAsr prayer. Then whoever prays ʿIsha will be forgiven what is between it and the Maghrib prayer. Then perhaps he may spend his night turning over; then if he rises, performs ablution, and prays Fajr, he will be forgiven what is between it and the ʿIsha prayer. These are the good deeds that remove evil deeds.'"

As for the evil deeds mentioned here, the commentators said: they are minor sins. And Muʿadh ibn Jabal narrated: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, advise me.' He said: 'Fear Allah wherever you are.' I said: 'Add to it.' He said: 'Follow the evil deed with a good deed, and it will erase it.' I said: 'Add to it.' He said: 'Deal with people with good character.'"

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That is a reminder for those who remember﴾. Regarding what is referred to by "that," there are three views:

One: it is the Qur'an. The second: the establishment of prayer. The third: all that preceded of the command to uprightness, the prohibition of transgression, not inclining toward the wrongdoers, and maintaining the prayer.

(p-170) Regarding what is meant by "reminder," there are two views:

One: it means repentance. The second: it means admonition.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And be patient﴾. Regarding what he was commanded to be patient upon, there are two opinions:

The first: patience over the harm he suffers from his people. The second: the prayer.

Regarding the intended meaning of "the good-doers" (al-muhsinin), there are three opinions:

The first: they are those who pray, related from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: they are the sincere (al-mukhlisun), related from Muqatil. The third: they are those who do good in their deeds, related from Abu Sulayman.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verse 116:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So why were there not among the generations before you those of remaining virtue﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Farra' said: the meaning is: "So there were not." Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning is: "Why was there not among the generations before you those of remaining virtue (ulu baqiyyah)?" Ibn Jammaz narrated from Abu Ja'far that it is read "ulu biqyah," with a kasra on the ba', sukun on the qaf, and the ya' lightened.

Regarding the meaning of "ulu baqiyyah" there are three opinions:

The first: they are people of religion (ulu din), said by Ibn ʿAbbas. Ibn Qutaybah said: It is said, "a people who have baqiyyah, and in whom there is baqiyyah," when there remains in them a trace (muskah) and there is goodness in them. The second: those of discernment (ulu tamyiz). The third: those of obedience (ulu ta'ah). Al-Zajjaj mentioned these two and said: When you say, "So-and-so has baqiyyah in him," its meaning is: there is excellence in him.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿except a few﴾. This is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati'), meaning: but a few of those whom We rescued from them, (p-171) who forbade corruption. Muqatil said: Among the generations there were none who forbade sins and polytheism except a few of those whom We rescued from the punishment together with the messengers.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who did wrong pursued what they had been given luxury in﴾. That is: along with their wrongdoing, they pursued what they had been given luxury in, while their bounties continued, so they did not accept what would diminish their luxury. Al-Farra' said: They preferred worldly pleasures over the matter of the Hereafter. He said: It is also said: they pursued their evil sins to the Fire.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verse 117:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly﴾, regarding this there are two views:

One: "unjustly" means without any wrongdoing (jurm). This was said by Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: "unjustly" means by way of shirk (polytheism). This was mentioned by Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) and Abu Sulayman.

Regarding His saying: ﴿while its people are reforming﴾, there are three views:

The first: they deal with one another equitably (yantasifu ba'duhum min ba'd, i.e. they give each other their due). This was narrated by Qays ibn Abi Hazim from Jarir. Abu Ja'far al-Tabari said: the meaning is that He does not destroy them when they act equitably among themselves, even if they are polytheists; He destroys them only when they wrong one another.

The second: they are reforming their deeds, holding firmly to obedience. This was said by Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: they are believers. This was said by Muqatil.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verses 118–119:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, He would have made mankind one community﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: If He had willed to make them all Muslims, He would have done so.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they will not cease to differ﴾. Regarding those referred to, there are two opinions:

The first: they are the people of truth and the people of falsehood. This was narrated by al-Ḍaḥḥak from Ibn ʿAbbas. The meaning would then be: these will oppose those.

The second: they are the people of desires (ahl al-ahwaʾ), who will not cease to differ. This was narrated by ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿAbbas.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Except those on whom your Lord has mercy﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: they are the people of truth. Al-Ḥasan said: the people of the mercy of Allah do not differ.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And for that He created them﴾. Regarding what the word "that" refers to, there are four opinions:

The first: it refers to what they are upon. Ibn ʿAbbas said: He created them as two groups: a group that is shown mercy and so does not differ, and a group that is not shown mercy and so differs.

The second: it refers to wretchedness and happiness. This was also said by Ibn ʿAbbas, and it was chosen by al-Zajjaj, who said: because their difference leads them to happiness and wretchedness. Ibn Jarir said: the lam in His saying "wa-li-dhalika" (and for that) has the meaning of "ʿala" (upon).

The third: it refers to the difference (ikhtilaf). This was narrated by Mubarak from al-Ḥasan.

The fourth: it refers to mercy. This was narrated by ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿAbbas, and ʿIkrimah, Mujahid, al-Ḍaḥḥak and Qatadah also said it. According to this, the meaning is: for His mercy He created those who do not differ in their religion.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: the word of your Lord has become binding: ﴿I will surely fill Hell﴾ with the disbelieving jinn and the disbelieving people.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verses 118–119:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, He would have made mankind one community﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: If He had willed to make them all Muslims, He would have done so.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they will not cease to differ﴾. Regarding those referred to, there are two opinions:

The first: they are the people of truth and the people of falsehood. This was narrated by al-Ḍaḥḥak from Ibn ʿAbbas. The meaning would then be: these will oppose those.

The third: it refers to the difference (ikhtilaf). This was narrated by Mubarak from al-Ḥasan.

The fourth: it refers to mercy. This was narrated by ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿAbbas, and ʿIkrimah, Mujahid, al-Ḍaḥḥak and Qatadah also said it. According to this, the meaning is: for His mercy He created those who do not differ in their religion.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: the word of your Lord has become binding: ﴿I will surely fill Hell﴾ with the disbelieving jinn and the disbelieving people.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verse 120:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We relate to you all﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "kullan" (كُلًّا) is in the accusative governed by "naqussu" (نَقُصُّ). The meaning is: We relate to you all that you need of the news of the Messengers. "Ma" (مَا) is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for "kull," so the meaning is: We relate to you that by which We make your heart firm (nuthabbitu bihi fu'adaka). The meaning of making the heart firm (tathbit al-fu'ad) here is the tranquillity of the heart, not that it was doubtful; rather, the more proof and evidence there is, the firmer the heart becomes.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And there has come to you in this the truth﴾. Regarding what is referred to by "hadhihi" (هَذِهِ, "this"), there are four opinions:

The first: that it is the surah. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Abu al-'Aliyah, and Shayban narrated it from Qatadah.

The second: that it is the world (al-dunya), so the meaning is: "and there has come to you in this world the truth." Sa'id narrated it from Qatadah, and from al-Hasan the like of the two opinions.

The third: that it is the stories mentioned.

The fourth: that it is this very verse. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned the two opinions.

Regarding what is meant by "al-haqq" (the truth) here, there are three opinions:

The first: that it is the clarification (al-bayan). The second: the truthfulness of the narratives and accounts. The third: prophethood (al-nubuwwah).

If it is said: Did not the truth come to him in the whole Qur'an? Why then did He single out this surah?

The answer: If we say that the truth is prophethood, then the reference of "hadhihi" is to the world, so the meaning is: "and there came to you in this world prophethood," and the difficulty is resolved. If we say that it is the surah, then regarding it there are four answers:

The first: that the intended truth is the clarification, and this surah gathered, in clarifying the destruction of the nations and explaining their outcome, what no other surah gathered; so the effect of the specification became evident. This is the view of some exegetes.

The second: that some truth is more emphatic than other truth in its manifestness to us and its obscurity to us, (p-174) and for this reason people say: "So-and-so is in the truth" when he is at death, even though he was not previously in falsehood, but to magnify what he is in. So it is as if the truth made clear in this surah is more manifest than other. This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

The third: that He singled out this surah with that to demonstrate its virtue, even though there is truth in other surahs as well. It is like His saying: ﴿And the middle prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 238], and His saying: ﴿and Jibril and Mika'il﴾ [al-Baqarah: 98]. This is the view of Ibn al-Anbari.

The fourth: that the meaning is: "and there came to you in this surah the truth, along with what came to you from the rest of the surahs." This was said by Ibn Jarir al-Tabari.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and an admonition and a reminder for the believers﴾, i.e., they are admonished when they hear this surah and what befell the nations, so their hearts soften.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verses 121–122:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And say to those who do not believe: "Work according to your position; indeed, we are working [according to ours]."﴾ This is a threat and a warning. The meaning is: do what you are doing, for you will soon know the outcome of your affair. ﴿And wait﴾ for what Satan promises you. ﴿Indeed, we are waiting﴾ for what our Lord promises us.

Section

The exegetes said: this verse required leaving them to their deeds and being content with warning them, and it is abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf).

Know that if we say that the purpose of the verse is a threat, then no abrogation applies to it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 11, verses 121–122:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And say to those who do not believe: "Work according to your position; indeed, we are working [according to ours]."﴾ This is a threat and a warning. The meaning is: do what you are doing, for you will soon know the outcome of your affair. ﴿And wait﴾ for what Satan promises you. ﴿Indeed, we are waiting﴾ for what our Lord promises us.

Section

The exegetes said: this verse required leaving them to their deeds and being content with warning them, and it is abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf).

Know that if we say that the purpose of the verse is a threat, then no abrogation applies to it.

(p-175) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾, i.e., the knowledge of what is hidden from the servants within them. ﴿And to Him the whole matter will be returned﴾. Nafi' and Hafs, from Asim, read "yurja'u al-amru kulluhu" with a dammah on the yā' (yuraja'u). The rest of the readers, and Abu Bakr from Asim, read "yarji'u" with a fathah on the yā' (yarji'u). The meaning: all matters return to Him on the Day of Return (al-ma'ad). ﴿So worship Him﴾, i.e., alone. ﴿And rely upon Him﴾, i.e., trust in Him. ﴿And your Lord is not unaware of what you do﴾. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs from Asim read "ta'malun" with a tā' (taʿmalūna). The rest read it with a yā' (yaʿmalūna). Abu 'Ali said: whoever reads with a yā', the meaning is: say to them, "Your Lord is not unaware of what they do." Whoever reads with a tā', the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) and to all creation, believers and disbelievers alike, so it is more general than the yā' reading. This is a warning, and the meaning is: He will repay the good-doer for his goodness and the wrongdoer for his wrongdoing. Ka'b said: the conclusion of the Torah is the conclusion of Surah Hud.
